dabhol.s: Dabhol is a historic port on the Konkan coast of western India. Under the Maratha Empire, ports such as Dabhol and Rajapur linked the Deccan to Arabian Sea trade networks.

dabiran.s: The dabiran were the class of scribes and administrators in the Sasanian Empire. They formed one of the four estates of Sasanian society, alongside priests, warriors and commoners, in a hierarchy formalised in Zoroastrian religious law.

dacia.s: Dacia was an ancient region north of the lower Danube, roughly corresponding to present-day Romania. The Roman emperor Trajan conquered it in two wars in 101–102 and 105–106 CE.

dadu.s: Dadu, also called Khanbaliq, was the capital of the Yuan Dynasty, built by Kublai Khan on the site of present-day Beijing. It was a planned imperial city that impressed visitors such as Marco Polo.

dagestan.s: Dagestan is a mountainous region on the western shore of the Caspian Sea in the northeastern Caucasus. Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire campaigned there at great cost against its highland peoples.

dai.s: A da'i, meaning "summoner", was a missionary and propagandist of the Ismaili movement. Da'is spread the Ismaili cause clandestinely across the Islamic world, and the da'i Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i won over the Kutama Berbers who brought the Fatimids to power.

daimyo.s: The daimyo were the great feudal lords of Japan who ruled domains and commanded samurai retainers. Under the Tokugawa Shogunate about 260 daimyo governed their domains semi-autonomously, subject to shogunal regulation and the system of alternate attendance in Edo.

dakar-adal.s: Dakar, or Dakkar, was a town in the Horn of Africa that served as a capital of the Adal Sultanate. The sultanate's administrative capital shifted from the coastal port of Zeila to Dakar and eventually to Harar.

dakar-senegal.s: Dakar is a port city on the Cap-Vert peninsula and the capital of present-day Senegal. It was the headquarters of French West Africa, one of the two great federations through which the French Empire governed its African colonies.

dalai-lama.s: The Dalai Lama is the title of the leading figure of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, later the head of the Tibetan government. The institution itself arose in the sixteenth century.

dali-kingdom.s: The Dali Kingdom was a state in present-day Yunnan in southwestern China, which lasted from the tenth to the thirteenth century. It was conquered by the Mongols under Kublai Khan in the 1250s.

dalmatia.s: Dalmatia is a historical region along the eastern Adriatic coast, in present-day Croatia. It came under Habsburg rule in the nineteenth century.

damanyima.s: Damanyima is a place named in Luba oral tradition as the northern limit of the early expansion of the Luba state. According to tradition, the founder Kalala Ilunga extended his realm north to Damanyima, west to the Bushime River and east to the Lufwa River.

damascus.s: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, now the capital of Syria. It was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, whose Great Mosque still stands there.

dambarare.s: Dambarare was a Portuguese trading settlement on the Zimbabwe plateau in the seventeenth century. It was destroyed by the forces of Changamire Dombo in the campaigns of the early 1690s.

danangombe.s: Danangombe is an archaeological site on the Zimbabwean plateau, known for its dry-stone enclosures. It was one of the principal centres of the Rozvi Empire, where the stone-walled complexes served as administrative headquarters, royal residences and ceremonial centres of the…

dano-swedish-wars.s: The Dano-Swedish wars were a long series of conflicts between Denmark-Norway and Sweden for control of Scandinavia and the Baltic. Fought intermittently from the break-up of the Kalmar Union into the early eighteenth century, they shaped the rise of the Swedish Empire, notably…

danube.s: The Danube is one of Europe's great rivers, flowing from southern Germany to the Black Sea. For the Roman Empire and later the Byzantine Empire it served as a major frontier and line of defence, while in the Carolingian Empire and the Austro-Hungarian Empire it functioned as…

darb-el-arbain.s: Darb el-Arba'in, the 'forty-day road', was a caravan route linking Darfur to Asyut in Upper Egypt. It was the commercial lifeline of the Darfur Sultanate, which developed and controlled it, and it carried slaves, ivory and other goods northwards as well as pilgrims bound for…

darfur-sultanate.s: The Darfur Sultanate was a Muslim state of the Fur people in what is now western Sudan, which flourished from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. Its economy rested on Fur agriculture in the Marrah highlands, slave raiding and trade along the Darb el-Arba'in route to…

daric.s: The daric was a gold coin of the Achaemenid Empire, introduced under Darius I. Of consistently high purity, it served as a prestigious medium of exchange and a tool of royal policy, used to pay troops and to subsidise allies and clients, including Greek states.

darius-i.s: Darius I, also known as Darius the Great, was king of the Achaemenid Empire (r. 522–486 BCE).

darius-ii.s: Darius II was a king of the Achaemenid Empire in the later fifth century BCE. His reign was marked by court intrigue, provincial revolts and Persian involvement in the later stages of the Peloponnesian War through subsidies to Sparta.

darius-iii.s: Darius III was the last king of the Achaemenid Empire. He was defeated by Alexander the Great at the battles of Issus and Gaugamela and was killed by his own officers in 330 BCE while fleeing eastward.

dariuss-scythian-campaign.s: Darius's Scythian campaign was a military expedition led by Darius I of the Achaemenid Empire against the Scythians north of the Black Sea in 513 BCE. The Persian army crossed the Bosporus and the Danube, but the nomadic Scythians avoided pitched battle and withdrew, forcing…

darya-i-noor.s: The Darya-i-Noor ('Sea of Light') is a large pale pink diamond, among the most famous gems in the world. It was taken from the Mughal treasury in Delhi by Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire, along with the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne, and carried back to Persia.

daulatabad.s: Daulatabad is a historic fortress city in the Deccan region of western India. In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughlaq of the Delhi Sultanate ordered the capital moved there from Delhi, intending to improve control of the southern provinces.

dawa.s: The da'wa ('summons' or 'mission') was the missionary and propaganda organisation of Ismaili Islam. Under the Fatimid Caliphate it was a hierarchical institution that spread Ismaili doctrine and loyalty to the imam-caliph across the Islamic world, playing a central role in the…

dawaro.s: Dawaro was a historic Muslim region and polity in the south-eastern highlands of present-day Ethiopia. It was incorporated into the Ethiopian Empire during the southward expansion of Amda Seyon I in the fourteenth century, alongside Bale and other Muslim sultanates.

dawit-i.s: Dawit I was an emperor of Ethiopia in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. His campaigns against the Muslim Ifat Sultanate led to the capture and execution of its ruler Sa'ad ad-Din II around 1410.

dawit-ii.s: Dawit II, also known as Lebna Dengel, was emperor of Ethiopia in the early sixteenth century. His forces were repeatedly defeated by Ahmad ibn Ibrahim of the Adal Sultanate, most decisively at the Battle of Amba Sel in 1531, after which he was driven into flight.

debre-damo.s: Debre Damo is an ancient monastery on a flat-topped mountain in northern Ethiopia, reachable only by rope. One of the oldest Christian institutions in the Ethiopian highlands, it is cited in the Adal Sultanate profile among the monasteries attacked during the conquests of…

deccan.s: The Deccan is the large plateau region of peninsular India south of the Narmada River. It was the heartland of the Maratha Empire, whose rise and military style were shaped by its hills and forts, and a persistent zone of conflict for the Mughal Empire.

deccan-plateau.s: The Deccan Plateau is the elevated tableland covering much of central and southern India. Its rugged, fortified uplands and semi-arid agriculture formed the geographic setting in which the Maratha Empire emerged, providing defensible strongholds and a base for the Maratha…

deccan-sultanates.s: The Deccan sultanates were a group of Muslim kingdoms, including Bijapur, Golconda and Ahmadnagar, that emerged in the Deccan after the break-up of the Bahmani Sultanate. The Maratha Empire grew out of this environment, as Maratha commanders such as Shahaji served the…

decimal-military-organisation.s: Decimal military organisation is a system of dividing an army into units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, each under its own commander. Common among steppe peoples, it was used by the Xiongnu Empire and later underpinned the armies of the Mongols and the Timurid…

decimal-system.s: The decimal system, or place-value notation, is a method of writing numbers using ten digits whose value depends on their position, including a symbol for zero. Its development in India is associated with the period of the Gupta Empire, when mathematicians such as Aryabhata…

decimal-system-mongol-army.s: The decimal system of the Mongol army organised troops into units of ten (arban), a hundred (jaghun), a thousand (mingghan) and ten thousand (tumen). Under Genghis Khan these units were deliberately mixed across tribal lines, breaking old loyalties and binding soldiers to the…

decolonisation.s: Decolonisation refers to the process by which colonies gained independence from imperial powers, especially in the decades after the Second World War. It brought the end of the British Empire and French Empire as global colonial systems, and the defeat of the Empire of Japan…

deflation.s: Deflation is a sustained fall in the general level of prices, often linked to a shortage of money. In the Qing Empire, a silver-based monetary economy depended on silver imports, and their disruption in the early nineteenth century produced deflationary pressures that worsened…

deforestation.s: Deforestation is the large-scale clearing of forests. In the Kushite Empire, deforestation linked to the fuel demands of iron production around Meroë is cited, together with possible shifts in Nile flooding, as an environmental factor that undermined the agricultural and…

deioces.s: Deioces was the traditional founder of the Median kingdom (r. c. 678–c.

dejima.s: Dejima was a small artificial island in the harbour of Nagasaki. Under the Tokugawa Shogunate's policy of restricted foreign contact, it was the sole place where the Dutch were permitted to trade with Japan.

delhi.s: Delhi is a city in northern India and one of the most important political centres of South Asian history. It was the capital of the Delhi Sultanate and, later, of the Mughal Empire, and was sacked by Timur in 1398 and by Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire in 1739.

delhi-sultanate.s: The Delhi Sultanate was a series of Muslim dynasties that ruled much of northern India from Delhi between the early thirteenth and early sixteenth centuries. It repelled Mongol incursions from the Chagatai realm, suffered Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398, and ended when Babur…

demak-sultanate.s: The Demak Sultanate was the first major Muslim state on Java, based on the island's north coast. Its rise in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries contributed to the final collapse of the Hindu-Buddhist Majapahit Empire and to the spread of Islam across Java.

demetrius-ii-nicator.s: Demetrius II Nicator was a king of the Seleucid Empire in the second century BCE. His reign was disrupted by dynastic rivals and by a war against the Parthians, who captured him and held him prisoner for years.

democratic-republic-of-the-congo.s: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is a large country in Central Africa. Its southern savanna, particularly the Katanga region, was the homeland of the Luba Empire and the Lunda Empire, whose political traditions and influence spread widely across the region.

denarius.s: The denarius was the standard silver coin of the Roman Empire for several centuries. Its progressive debasement in the third century was a sign of fiscal crisis.

dendi.s: Dendi is a region along the Niger River in the south-east of present-day Niger and northern Benin. After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 shattered the Songhai Empire, the Songhai royal family retreated there and maintained a rump state for decades.

denkyira.s: Denkyira was an Akan state in what is now southern Ghana that dominated the region in the seventeenth century, holding the Asante as tributaries. Its defeat by the Asante under Osei Tutu at the Battle of Feyiase in 1701 marked the emergence of the Ashanti Empire as the leading…

denmark.s: Denmark is a Scandinavian kingdom that, as Denmark-Norway, was Sweden's principal rival for control of the Baltic in the early modern period. Swedish victories over Denmark, culminating in the Treaty of Roskilde (1658), were central to the foundation of the Swedish Empire,…

deodoro-da-fonseca.s: Deodoro da Fonseca was a Brazilian army officer who led the military coup of 15 November 1889 that overthrew Emperor Pedro II. He proclaimed the republic and became the first president of Brazil, ending the Brazilian Empire.

departement.s: A département is an administrative division of France created in 1790 to replace the old provinces with uniform units. The French Empire extended the system to conquered lands and to Algeria after 1848.

department-of-state-affairs.s: The Department of State Affairs was one of the three departments in the Tang Dynasty's 'three departments and six ministries' system of government. Alongside the Secretariat and the Chancellery, it formed part of a structure of overlapping checks on policy, and it supervised…

dependence-on-a-single-ruler.s: Dependence on a single ruler describes the vulnerability of states whose power rested on the personal ability of one leader rather than on durable institutions. Such empires often expanded rapidly but fragmented when that ruler died or was overthrown.

depopulation-and-demographic-collapse.s: Depopulation and demographic collapse refers to sharp falls in population caused by epidemic disease, war, famine or slave raiding, which undermined the economic and military base of states. Examples include the Aztec Empire, devastated by epidemics after the Spanish conquest,…

deportation.s: Deportation refers to the forced removal of people from their homes to other places. Mass deportation was a systematic tool of the Assyrian Empire and the Chaldean Empire, used to break resistance and redistribute labour, most famously in the Babylonian exile of the Judeans.

deportation-and-population-transfer.s: Deportation and population transfer describes the recurring imperial practice of forcibly moving conquered populations to suppress resistance, resettle land and supply labour. The Assyrian Empire used it on a vast scale, and the Chaldean Empire continued it with the Babylonian…

deportation-of-armenians-to-new-julfa.n: Deportation of Armenians to New Julfa
deportation-of-armenians-to-new-julfa.s: The deportation of Armenians to New Julfa was the forced relocation of Armenians from Julfa and other districts by Shah Abbas I of the Safavid Empire in 1604–1605. Resettled in a new quarter of Isfahan, the Armenian merchants of New Julfa became central to Safavid silk and…

derg.s: The Derg was the military committee that seized power in Ethiopia, formed in 1974. It deposed Emperor Haile Selassie that year, ending the Ethiopian Empire and the Solomonic monarchy, and went on to rule as a Marxist-Leninist regime that nationalised land and carried out…

desiderius.s: Desiderius was the last king of the Lombards in Italy. His conflicts with the papacy led Pope Adrian I to appeal to Charlemagne, who besieged Pavia and conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774.

destruction-of-dambarare.s: The destruction of Dambarare was the capture and destruction of a Portuguese trading settlement on the Zimbabwean plateau in 1693 by forces of Changamire Dombo. It formed part of a rapid campaign by the Rozvi Empire that eliminated the Portuguese interior settlements and…

destruction-of-eshnunna.s: The destruction of Eshnunna was the final defeat of the Mesopotamian city-state of Eshnunna by Hammurabi of the Babylonian Empire around 1755 BCE. According to the site's account, it was achieved by damming the city's water supply rather than by direct assault, an example of…

destruction-of-mari.s: The destruction of Mari refers to the sack of the city of Mari on the Middle Euphrates by Hammurabi of the Babylonian Empire in 1761 BCE. Mari, once an ally of Babylon under King Zimri-Lim, was conquered and its palace destroyed, removing a powerful rival.

destruction-of-susa.s: The destruction of Susa was the sack of the Elamite capital by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal around 647 BCE. The Assyrian Empire's armies looted and razed the city, desecrated royal tombs and deported population, effectively ending Elam as a major power.

devaraja.s: Devaraja ('god-king') was a religious and political concept associating the ruler with a divine power, usually Shiva. It was central to the Khmer Empire from its foundation under Jayavarman II, legitimising royal authority and the building of state temples such as those at…

devshirme.s: The devshirme was the Ottoman system of levying boys, mainly from Christian families in the Balkans, who were converted to Islam and trained for state service. The ablest entered the palace administration, while most joined the Janissary corps.

dhar-tichitt.s: Dhar Tichitt is an escarpment in south-central Mauritania with extensive remains of stone-built settlements. The Tichitt culture, traceable to around 1600 BCE, is regarded by the site as the archaeological forerunner of the Ghana Empire and the Soninke people who built it.

dhar-walata.s: Dhar Walata is an escarpment in south-eastern Mauritania with archaeological remains of the Tichitt stone-settlement culture. Together with Dhar Tichitt, it is cited as evidence of the early settled societies from which the Ghana Empire emerged.

dharma.s: Dharma is a central concept in Indian religions, denoting moral law, duty and righteous conduct. Under the Maurya Empire, Ashoka promoted dharma as a principle of government after the Kalinga war, proclaiming ethical rules, tolerance and welfare through edicts inscribed across…

dhian-singh.s: Dhian Singh was a Dogra noble who served as wazir (chief minister) of the Sikh Empire. After the death of Ranjit Singh in 1839, he and his brothers were leading figures among the factions of the Lahore Darbar, and he was killed in 1843 amid the violent succession struggles…

dhimmi.s: Dhimmi is the status under Islamic law of protected non-Muslim communities, mainly Christians and Jews, who were permitted to practise their religion in return for paying a poll tax (jizya) and accepting certain restrictions. It structured relations between rulers and subject…

dhu-nuwas.s: Dhu Nuwas was a Jewish king of Himyar in South Arabia in the early sixth century, remembered for his persecution of Christians at Najran. The Aksumite Empire, at the request of the Byzantine emperor, sent a naval expedition across the Red Sea that defeated him and installed a…

diadochi.s: The Diadochi ('successors') were the generals and companions of Alexander the Great who fought over his empire after his death in 323 BCE. Their wars broke up the Macedonian Empire and produced the Hellenistic kingdoms, including the Ptolemaic Empire in Egypt, founded by…

dido.s: Dido, also called Elissa, was the legendary queen from Tyre who is said to have founded Carthage. According to tradition, she fled her brother Pygmalion and established the city on the North African coast.

digest-justinian.s: The Digest is a compilation of extracts from the writings of classical Roman jurists, issued in 533 under Emperor Justinian I. It forms a major part of the Corpus Juris Civilis, the codification of Roman law undertaken in the Byzantine Empire.

dihqan.s: The dihqans were the Persian landed gentry of the Sasanian era, who managed villages and collected taxes. After the Arab conquests, the Umayyad Caliphate relied on them as local intermediaries for tax collection and administration in Iran and Iraq, preserving much of the…

dil-naod.s: Dil Na'od is remembered as the last king of the Aksumite dynasty. According to the site's account, he was overthrown around 940 CE by his own general Mara Takla Haymanot, who founded the Zagwe dynasty.

dilmun.s: Dilmun was an ancient trading land in the Persian Gulf, generally identified with Bahrain and the adjacent coast. It acted as an intermediary in the trade between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, and Akkadian royal inscriptions refer to ships from Dilmun docking at Akkad,…

dinar.s: The dinar was the gold coin of the Islamic world, first issued in the Umayyad period. Almoravid gold dinars, minted from West African gold carried across the Sahara, were among the most trusted coins of the western Mediterranean and circulated widely.

dinga-cisse.s: Dinga Cissé is a figure of Soninke oral tradition credited with unifying the clans that formed the Ghana Empire, known as Wagadou. He is regarded as the legendary ancestor of the Cissé ruling lineage, and his story stands at the beginning of the empire's traditional history.

diocletian.s: Diocletian was Roman emperor (r. 284–305 CE) who ended the third-century crisis.

diogo-cao.s: Diogo Cão was a Portuguese navigator who explored the coast of west-central Africa in the 1480s. He reached the mouth of the Congo River around 1483, establishing the first contact between Portugal and the Kongo Empire.

diplomacy-and-marriage-alliances.s: Diplomacy and marriage alliances describes the use of treaties, gifts and dynastic marriages to win allies, legitimise rule and expand influence without war. The Gupta Empire benefited from Chandragupta I's marriage into the Licchavi clan, the Mitanni Empire sent royal…

diplomatic-marriage.s: Diplomatic marriage is the practice of arranging royal marriages to seal alliances between states. The Mitanni Empire made extensive use of it, sending princesses to the pharaohs of Egypt, as recorded in the Amarna letters.

dirham.s: The dirham was the silver coin of the Islamic world. Large quantities of Abbasid and other dirhams flowed northwards along trade routes controlled by the Khazar Khaganate, reaching the Volga region, Eastern Europe and Scandinavia.

dissolution-of-the-holy-roman-empire.n: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
dissolution-of-the-holy-roman-empire.s: The dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire took place in 1806, when Emperor Francis II abdicated the imperial title following Napoleon's victories and the creation of the Confederation of the Rhine. It brought an end to an institution that had existed for about a thousand years…

divan.s: The Divan was the imperial council of the Ottoman Empire, chaired by the grand vizier. It brought together the viziers, military judges, treasurers and the chancellor to deal with state affairs, legal cases and petitions.

divided-succession-and-partible-inherita.s: Divided succession and partible inheritance describes the practice of dividing a realm among a ruler's heirs rather than passing it intact to one successor. It frequently produced civil war and fragmentation.

divine-kingship.s: Divine kingship is the idea that a ruler is a god or possesses divine status. Naram-Sin of the Akkadian Empire claimed divinity, the Khmer Empire built its state around the devaraja cult, and rulers of the Benin Empire held sacred status.

diwan.s: The diwan was a register and administrative office in Islamic states. Established under Caliph Umar around 636 CE, it recorded the names of Muslim soldiers and their stipends, financed by conquest revenues, and became the basis of the Rashidun Caliphate's and Umayyad…

diwan-dina-nath.s: Diwan Dina Nath was a senior official of the Sikh Empire who managed its financial administration, succeeding Diwan Mohkam Chand. As part of Ranjit Singh's multiethnic and multireligious administrative elite, he remained an influential figure at the Lahore Darbar.

diwan-mohkam-chand.s: Diwan Mohkam Chand was a leading official and military commander of the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh. He managed financial administration and was among the multiethnic and multireligious elite through which Ranjit Singh governed.

diyarbakir.s: Diyarbakir, the ancient Amida, is a city in south-eastern Anatolia on the upper Tigris. It was a key fortress on the frontier between Rome and Persia, captured by the Sasanian Empire under Shapur II in 359 CE after a siege.

djenne.s: Djenné is a city in the inland Niger Delta of present-day Mali, famous for its mud-brick Great Mosque. A major centre of trade and Islamic learning, it linked the forest zone to the trans-Saharan network.

dmitry-milyutin.s: Dmitry Milyutin was a Russian statesman who served as War Minister from 1861 to 1881. He carried out sweeping military reforms in the Russian Empire, including the reorganisation of the army into military districts, improved officer training and the introduction of universal…

dnieper.s: The Dnieper is a major river of Eastern Europe, flowing through present-day Russia, Belarus and Ukraine to the Black Sea. It was a central route of trade linking Scandinavia and the Rus' to Byzantium.

dodecanese.s: The Dodecanese is a group of islands in the south-eastern Aegean Sea. Italy seized them from the Ottoman Empire during the Italo-Turkish War of 1911–1912, and they remained part of the Italian Empire until after the Second World War, when they were transferred to Greece.

dogras.s: The Dogras are a people of the Jammu region in northern India. Dogra brothers, notably Gulab Singh and Dhian Singh, rose to great power at the court of the Sikh Empire, and after Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 their factional manoeuvres contributed to the instability that led to…

dome-of-soltaniyeh.s: The Dome of Soltaniyeh is the mausoleum of the Ilkhanid ruler Öljaitü at Sultaniyya in north-western Iran, completed around 1313. Its huge double-shelled brick dome is one of the great achievements of Persian architecture and a major monument of the Ilkhanate's cultural legacy.

dome-of-the-rock.s: The Dome of the Rock is an Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, built under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik in the late seventh century. After Saladin recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187, the Ayyubid Empire restored it as a Muslim holy site, and it…

dominate.s: The Dominate is the term for the later form of government of the Roman Empire, usually dated from the reign of Diocletian. In contrast to the earlier Principate, the emperor ruled openly as an absolute monarch (dominus), surrounded by court ceremonial and a large bureaucracy.

dominican-order.s: The Dominican Order is a Catholic order of friars founded by Saint Dominic in the early thirteenth century, dedicated to preaching and study. In the Spanish Empire, Dominican friars such as Bartolomé de las Casas criticised the abuse and enslavement of indigenous Americans,…

dominion.s: A dominion was a self-governing territory of the British Empire, such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. The dominions had elected parliaments and substantial autonomy, and the Statute of Westminster (1931) granted them full legislative independence.

dominus-et-deus.s: Dominus et deus ('lord and god') was a title associated with certain Roman emperors, notably Domitian, who is reported to have wished to be addressed in this way. It reflects the trend towards autocratic and sacralised rule in the Roman Empire that culminated in the Dominate.

donbas.s: The Donbas is a region of coal and heavy industry in the basin of the Donets River, in present-day eastern Ukraine. In the late nineteenth century it became one of the main centres of industrialisation in the Russian Empire, with rapid growth of coal mining and iron and steel…

donghu.s: The Donghu ('Eastern Hu') were a nomadic confederation in the steppe east of the Xiongnu. Around the time of the Xiongnu Empire's foundation, Modu Chanyu defeated and destroyed them, absorbing their territory and people.

doud-murra.s: Doud Murra was the last independent sultan of Wadai (r. 1898–1901, 1903–1909).

drogon-chogyal-phagpa.s: Drogön Chögyal Phagpa was a Tibetan Buddhist lama of the Sakya school who became imperial preceptor to Kublai Khan. In the Yuan Dynasty he was given authority over Buddhist affairs and over Tibet, and he devised the 'Phags-pa script, intended as a common writing system for the…

drought-and-climate-change.s: Drought and climate change refers to environmental shifts, such as prolonged droughts, cooling or failing monsoons, that undermined harvests, pastures and state revenues. Such pressures are linked to the collapse of the Akkadian Empire, the decline of the Khmer Empire and the…

dry-stone-construction.s: Dry-stone construction is a building technique in which walls are made from carefully fitted stones without mortar. On the Zimbabwean plateau it was the hallmark of Great Zimbabwe, and the Rozvi Empire revived the tradition, building fine dry-stone enclosures at Danangombe,…

dual-kingship.s: Dual kingship is a system in which authority is divided between two rulers. In the Khazar Khaganate, the khagan held a sacred, largely ceremonial position while a second ruler, often called the bek, exercised practical military and administrative power.

dughlat.s: The Dughlat were a powerful Mongol tribal confederation in Central Asia. Within the Chagatai Empire and its eastern successor, Moghulistan, Dughlat leaders often held the real power, installing and controlling khans whose authority depended on tribal military support.

duke-of-saxony.s: The Duke of Saxony was the ruler of the duchy of Saxony in the Holy Roman Empire. Under the Golden Bull of 1356 the Duke of Saxony was one of the seven prince-electors entitled to elect the emperor, alongside the archbishops of Mainz, Trier and Cologne, the King of Bohemia,…

duleep-singh.s: Duleep Singh was the last maharaja of the Sikh Empire, installed as a child after the violent succession struggles that followed Ranjit Singh's death. After the Anglo-Sikh wars the British annexed the Punjab in 1849, and he was removed to Britain, where he spent most of his…

dunama-dabbalemi.s: Dunama Dabbalemi was a ruler (mai) of Kanem (r. c. 1221–1259).

dungan-revolt.s: The Dungan Revolt was a major uprising of Muslim Hui and other peoples in north-western China in the 1860s and 1870s. It devastated Shaanxi and Gansu and led to the temporary loss of Xinjiang before Qing forces under Zuo Zongtang reconquered the region.

durrani-empire.s: The Durrani Empire was an Afghan state founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747 after the death of Nader Shah of the Afsharid Empire. It raided northern India repeatedly, defeated the Maratha Empire at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 and further weakened the Mughal Empire.

dutch.s: The Dutch are the people of the Netherlands, who became a leading maritime and commercial power in the seventeenth century. Through the Dutch Empire and its trading companies they competed with the Portuguese Empire and the Spanish Empire, traded with Japan under the Tokugawa…

dutch-conquest-of-the-banda-islands.n: Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands
dutch-conquest-of-the-banda-islands.s: The Dutch conquest of the Banda Islands was the seizure of these nutmeg-producing islands in 1621 by the Dutch East India Company under Jan Pieterszoon Coen. Most of the native population was killed, enslaved or driven out, and the islands were resettled with plantations…

dutch-east-india-company.s: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was a chartered trading company founded in 1602, with powers to wage war, make treaties and govern territory in Asia. It was the main instrument of the Dutch Empire in the East Indies, displaced the Portuguese Empire from much of the spice…

dutch-empire.s: The Dutch Empire was the overseas colonial and commercial empire of the Netherlands, built mainly from the seventeenth century by the Dutch East India Company and the Dutch West India Company. Centred on the East Indies, it also included trading posts and colonies in Africa,…

dutch-republic.s: The Dutch Republic was the federal state of the United Provinces of the Netherlands that emerged from the revolt against Spain in the late sixteenth century. A leading commercial and naval power in the seventeenth century, it was a model and rival for England, and its…

dutch-revolt.s: The Dutch Revolt was the uprising of the Netherlands against Spanish Habsburg rule that began in the 1560s and led to the independence of the Dutch Republic. It drained the resources of the Spanish Empire, and because Portugal was united with the Spanish crown from 1580 to…

dutch-west-india-company.s: The Dutch West India Company was a chartered company established in 1621 to conduct Dutch trade and warfare in the Atlantic. It played a central role in the Dutch Empire's activities in West Africa, Brazil, the Caribbean and North America, including the Atlantic slave trade,…

duwa.s: Duwa was a khan of the Chagatai Khanate in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. An ally of Kaidu in the wars against the Yuan, he also directed raids into India against the Delhi Sultanate.

dvoryanstvo.s: The dvoryanstvo was the hereditary nobility of the Russian Empire. Originally a service class bound to the tsar, it gained extensive privileges in the eighteenth century, including exemption from compulsory service, and dominated land ownership and the serf economy until the…

dwarasamudra.s: Dwarasamudra, modern Halebidu in Karnataka, was the capital of the Hoysala kingdom in southern India. In the early fourteenth century Malik Kafur, general of the Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khalji, extracted enormous tribute from the Hoysalas there during his southern…

dwight-d-eisenhower.s: Dwight D. Eisenhower was a US general and President of the United States from 1953 to 1961.

dzud.s: Dzud is a Mongolian term for a catastrophic winter, when heavy snow, ice or extreme cold prevents livestock from grazing and causes mass deaths of animals. Severe dzud and droughts in the first century BCE killed great numbers of livestock and brought famine to the steppe,…

dzungar-genocide.s: The Dzungar genocide was the mass killing of the Dzungar Oirat Mongols by Qing forces in 1755–1757 under the Qianlong Emperor. Together with epidemics and flight, it destroyed most of the Dzungar population and ended the Dzungar Khanate, allowing the Qing Empire to incorporate…

dzungaria.s: Dzungaria is a region of northern Xinjiang in north-western China, between the Altai and Tianshan mountains. It was the heartland of the Dzungar Khanate, a long-standing rival of the Qing Empire, until the Qing conquest of the 1750s brought it under Chinese rule.

dzungars.s: The Dzungars were a confederation of Oirat Mongol tribes who formed the last great nomadic empire of Inner Asia in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. They fought a series of wars with the Qing Empire over Mongolia, Tibet and Central Asia, until the Qing destroyed their…

deccan-states-agency.s: The Deccan States Agency was a political agency of British India formed in 1933 to supervise the princely states of the Deccan and the Southern Maratha Country, many of them ruled by Maratha families. It was attached to Kolhapur.

delagoa-bay.s: Delagoa Bay, now Maputo Bay, is a large natural harbour on the coast of southern Mozambique. From the 16th century Portuguese, Dutch, Austrian and British traders competed for its ivory trade with the Tembe and other local chiefdoms.

dmitry-donskoy.s: Dmitry Donskoy was Grand Prince of Moscow from 1359 and of Vladimir from 1362. He built the first stone Kremlin in Moscow and made Moscow the leading Russian principality over Tver and Ryazan.

dayan-khan.s: Dayan Khan, Batu Möngke, was a Borjigin khan of the Northern Yuan who reunited the eastern Mongols in the late 15th and early 16th centuries, with the help of his queen Mandukhai. He defeated the Oirats and rebellious chiefs and divided the Mongols into six tümen ruled by his…

divrigi-great-mosque-and-hospital.s: The Divriği Great Mosque and Hospital is a joined mosque and hospital in eastern Anatolia, built in 1228–1229 by the Mengujekid ruler Ahmad Shah and his wife Turan Malik. It is famous for the richly carved stone portals, unlike any other Seljuk-era building.

diarmait-mac-murchada.s: Diarmait Mac Murchada was King of Leinster of the Uí Chennselaig dynasty. Driven out by the High King Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair and Tigernán Ua Ruairc in 1166, he sought help from Henry II of England and recruited Anglo-Norman knights, above all Richard de Clare, known as…

duke-of-zhou.s: The Duke of Zhou, Ji Dan, was a brother of King Wu, founder of the Zhou dynasty. After Wu's early death he acted as regent for the young King Cheng, crushed the rebellion of the Three Guards and the Shang prince Wu Geng, and organised the granting of new states such as Lu, Wey…

dorians.s: The Dorians were one of the main divisions of the ancient Greeks, speaking the Doric dialect. Greek tradition told of their arrival in the Peloponnese with the return of the Heracleidae after the Trojan War.

dorian-hexapolis.s: The Dorian Hexapolis was a league of six Dorian Greek cities in south-west Anatolia and the nearby islands: Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros on Rhodes, Kos, Knidos and Halicarnassus. Its members met at the sanctuary of Triopian Apollo near Knidos for festivals and games.

dost-mohammad-khan.s: Dost Mohammad Khan was the founder of the Barakzai dynasty of Afghanistan. He took Kabul in 1826 and assumed the title of emir in 1834.

dost-mohammad-khan-of-bhopal.s: Dost Mohammad Khan was an Afghan soldier from Tirah who served in the Mughal army and, as imperial authority weakened after Aurangzeb's death in 1707, carved out his own state in Malwa. He built a fort at Islamnagar, developed Bhopal into his capital and became the first nawab…

date-masamune.s: Date Masamune was a daimyo of north-eastern Japan, known as the 'one-eyed dragon'. He expanded the Date lands in Mutsu but submitted to Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1590 and later sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu.

david-livingstone.s: David Livingstone was a Scottish missionary and explorer of central and southern Africa. He worked among the Tswana, reached Lake Ngami in 1849, crossed the continent from Luanda to the Indian Ocean between 1853 and 1856, and explored the Zambezi and Lake Malawi.

dinh-tien-hoang.s: Đinh Tiên Hoàng, born Đinh Bộ Lĩnh, was a local leader from Hoa Lư who defeated the rival warlords of the Twelve Warlords period. In 968 he proclaimed himself emperor, named the state Đại Cồ Việt and built a fortified capital at Hoa Lư.

duchy-of-lower-lorraine.s: The Duchy of Lower Lorraine was the northern half of Lotharingia, created when Archbishop Bruno of Cologne divided the duchy in 959. It covered much of the Low Countries and the lower Rhine, but its dukes had little power over counts such as those of Louvain, Limburg and Loon.

dae-yeon-rim.s: Dae Yeon-rim was a descendant of Dae Joyeong, founder of Balhae, and an officer of the Khitan Liao dynasty at Dongjing, modern Liaoyang. In 1029 he rebelled and proclaimed the state of Heungyo to revive Balhae, seeking help from Goryeo.

dagestan-oblast.s: The Dagestan Oblast was a province of the Russian Empire in the eastern Caucasus, created in 1860 after the defeat of Imam Shamil. The local khanates and shamkhalate were gradually abolished and their lands turned into districts under military administration.

dai-la.s: Đại La was a walled citadel on the site of modern Hanoi, the seat of Chinese governors of the Tang Protectorate General to Pacify the South and later of local rulers. It was rebuilt by the Tang general Gao Pian in the 860s.

demetrius-i-of-macedon.s: Demetrius I, called Poliorcetes, 'the Besieger', was a Macedonian general, son of Antigonus I. He freed Athens in 307 BCE and besieged Rhodes in 305–304 BCE with huge siege engines, without success.

deo-van-long.s: Deo Van Long was a White Tai chief from Lai Châu in north-western Vietnam who allied with the French against the Viet Minh. In 1948 France made him head of the autonomous Tai Federation.

dou-jiande.s: Dou Jiande was a rebel leader during the collapse of the Sui dynasty who built a kingdom called Xia on the Hebei plain, known for its humane treatment of captives. Marching to relieve Wang Shichong at Luoyang in 621, he was defeated and captured by Li Shimin at the Battle of…

du-wenxiu.s: Du Wenxiu was the leader of the Panthay Rebellion of Hui Muslims in Yunnan against the Qing dynasty. In 1856 he took Dali and ruled western Yunnan as Sultan Suleiman of the Pingnan state for sixteen years.

duke-huan-of-qi.s: Duke Huan of Qi ruled the state of Qi in eastern China from 685 to 643 BCE. With his minister Guan Zhong he reformed government and the economy and became the first of the hegemons of the Spring and Autumn period.

durad-brankovic.s: Đurađ Branković was Despot of Serbia from 1427 to 1456. He built the great fortress of Smederevo as his capital on the Danube, balancing between Hungary and the Ottomans.

daijo-kan.s: The Daijō-kan, or Great Council of State, was the supreme organ of government in ritsuryō Japan, set up under the Taihō Code of 701 and earlier codes. Headed by the chancellor and the ministers of the left and right, it supervised eight ministries and the provincial governors.

dae-joyeong.s: Dae Joyeong was the founder of Balhae, a kingdom of Manchuria and northern Korea. A former Goguryeo general, he led Goguryeo refugees and Mohe tribesmen out of Tang control, defeated a Tang army at Tianmenling in 698 and founded his state at Mount Dongmou in Manchuria.

dakshina-kosala.s: Dakshina Kosala, 'southern Kosala', was the historical name of the upper Mahanadi valley in what is now Chhattisgarh and western Odisha. It was ruled by the Sharabhapuriyas and then the Panduvamshis, whose capital Sirpur has major brick temples and Buddhist monasteries, and…

dal-cais.s: The Dál gCais were an Irish dynasty of north Munster, with lands in modern County Clare and Limerick. Originally minor, they rose in the 10th century under Mathgamain and his brother Brian Boru, who took Norse Limerick and Cashel and became high king of Ireland.

danishmend-gazi.s: Danishmend Gazi was a Turkmen leader who founded the Danishmendid principality in central and north-eastern Anatolia after the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071, taking Sivas, Tokat and Amasya. His exploits against the Byzantines inspired the Danishmendname, a Turkish heroic…

davi-canabarro.s: Davi Canabarro was a gaúcho military leader of the Ragamuffin War in southern Brazil. As a general of the Riograndense Republic he led the invasion of Santa Catarina with Giuseppe Garibaldi in 1839, which created the short-lived Juliana Republic.

david.s: David was, according to the Hebrew Bible, the second king of the united kingdom of Israel and Judah, successor of Saul and father of Solomon, who made Jerusalem his capital. He is remembered as warrior, psalmist and founder of the royal line of Judah.

david-of-trebizond.s: David of Trebizond was the last emperor of Trebizond, reigning from 1459. He sought a Christian and Turkmen alliance against the Ottomans, but in 1461 Mehmed II besieged Trebizond and David surrendered it, ending the last Byzantine successor state.

david-of-makuria.s: David was a king of Makuria, the Christian Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile, in the 1270s. He raided Aswan and the Red Sea port of Aidhab, provoking the Mamluk sultan Baybars, whose army defeated him in 1276 and placed a rival on the throne.

david-iv-of-georgia.s: David IV of Georgia, known as the Builder, became king in 1089 and stopped paying tribute to the Seljuks. He reformed the army and the church, annexed Kakheti-Hereti and Lori, and defeated a large Seljuk coalition at Didgori in 1121.

dawud-pasha.s: Dawud Pasha was the last Mamluk governor of Baghdad, ruling from 1817 to 1831. A Georgian-born former slave, he built factories, printing works and a modern-style army, and dealt as an equal with the British.

deir-el-bahari.s: Deir el-Bahari is a bay of cliffs on the west bank of the Nile opposite Luxor, site of the mortuary temples of Mentuhotep II of the 11th Dynasty and of Hatshepsut, whose terraced temple bears reliefs of the expedition to Punt. In the tomb DB320 nearby, priests of the 21st…

devanampiya-tissa.s: Devanampiya Tissa was a king of Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE and a contemporary and ally of the Maurya emperor Ashoka. According to the Mahavamsa, the monk Mahinda, Ashoka's son, converted him to Buddhism, and a sapling of the Bodhi tree was planted in…

dewa-agung-jambe.s: Dewa Agung Jambe was the Balinese king who restored the senior royal dynasty after the court of Gelgel was overthrown by the rebel Gusti Agung Maruti. Around 1686 he set up a new palace at Klungkung, also called Semarapura.

dhana-nanda.s: Dhana Nanda was the last king of the Nanda dynasty of Magadha in northern India. Greek accounts of Alexander's campaign speak of the great army of the eastern king, which helped turn Alexander's troops back at the Beas in 326 BCE.

di-xin.s: Di Xin was the last king of the Shang dynasty of China. Later Zhou tradition portrayed him as a cruel tyrant devoted to drink and his consort Daji, justifying his overthrow.

diet-of-worms.s: The Diet of Worms was the imperial assembly held in 1521 by the young Emperor Charles V at Worms. Martin Luther appeared before it and refused to recant his writings.

diet-of-worms-1495.s: The Diet of Worms of 1495, held under Maximilian I, launched the Imperial Reform of the Holy Roman Empire. It proclaimed the Eternal Public Peace, banning private feuds, created the Imperial Chamber Court and introduced a general imperial tax, the Common Penny.

diktaean-zeus.s: Diktaean Zeus was a form of Zeus worshipped in eastern Crete, linked with the myth of the god's birth and upbringing in a Cretan cave. His main sanctuary lay near Palaikastro, where the Hymn of the Kouretes was found.

din-eidyn.s: Din Eidyn was the Brittonic name of the fortress on the rock of Edinburgh, the chief stronghold of the post-Roman kingdom of Gododdin. The Welsh poem Y Gododdin describes its war band feasting there before the doomed attack on Catraeth.

domnall-brecc.s: Domnall Brecc was a king of Dál Riata of the Cenél nGabráin, grandson of Áedán mac Gabráin. He broke the alliance with the Uí Néill and was defeated at Mag Rath in Ireland in 637, losing Dál Riata's lands there.

dong-son-culture.s: The Đông Sơn culture was a Bronze Age culture of the Red River and Ma River valleys of northern Vietnam, named after a village in Thanh Hóa province. It is best known for large decorated bronze drums, traded widely across South-east Asia.

dong-yi.s: Dong Yi was a Qin commander who urged Zhang Han to surrender to Xiang Yu in 207 BCE. In the division of 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Di in northern Shaanxi, one of the Three Qins.

drabya-shah.s: Drabya Shah was the founder of the Gorkha Kingdom in the hills of central Nepal. A younger son of the ruler of Lamjung, he seized Gorkha in 1559 from its Khadka chief and became its first king of the Shah dynasty.

duan-siping.s: Duan Siping was the founder of the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan, a commander of Bai descent. In 937, with the help of allies from the eastern Yunnan tribes, he overthrew the Da Yining regime of Yang Ganzhen and proclaimed his own dynasty at Dali.

duan-ye.s: Duan Ye was a Chinese official of the Later Liang state in the Hexi Corridor whom the Lushuihu chief Juqu Mengxun proclaimed ruler in 397, founding the Northern Liang. A scholarly man with little real power, he was overthrown and killed by Juqu Mengxun in 401, after which the…

duke-huan-of-zheng.s: Duke Huan of Zheng was a younger brother of King Xuan of Zhou, who enfeoffed him with Zheng in the Wei valley in 806 BCE. Foreseeing the collapse of the Western Zhou, he moved his family and wealth east towards the Yellow River.

duong-dinh-nghe.s: Dương Đình Nghệ was a Vietnamese military leader who expelled the Southern Han forces from the Red River delta in 931 and governed it as an autonomous military governor of Tĩnh Hải circuit. He was murdered in 937 by his officer Kiều Công Tiễn, whose call for Southern Han help…

dionysius-i-of-syracuse.s: Dionysius I was tyrant of Syracuse from 405 to 367 BCE and the most powerful Greek ruler in the west of his time. He fought repeated wars against Carthage for control of Sicily, besieging and destroying Motya in 397 BCE with siege towers and the newly invented catapult.

duke-xian-of-jin.s: Duke Xian of Jin was ruler of the state of Jin in northern China during the Spring and Autumn period. He greatly expanded Jin by conquering neighbouring states, most famously in 655 BCE, when after bribing the State of Yu to let his army pass he destroyed Guo and then Yu itself.

diego-de-landa.s: Diego de Landa was a Spanish Franciscan friar and later Bishop of Yucatán. In 1562 he led an inquisition against Maya converts suspected of idolatry and burnt Maya codices and images at Maní.

duchy-of-naples.s: The Duchy of Naples was a Byzantine province on the Bay of Naples that became a largely independent state under its own dukes in the 8th century, while nominally recognising the emperor. It resisted the Lombards of Benevento and Arab raiders.

da-lat.s: Da Lat is a city on the Lang Biang plateau in Vietnam's Central Highlands, founded by the French in the 1890s as a hill station on the recommendation of Alexandre Yersin. Its cool climate made it a resort for colonial officials, and the last emperor, Bao Dai, kept a summer…

da-nang.s: Da Nang is a port city in central Vietnam, on a sheltered bay south of the Hai Van Pass. A French and Spanish fleet attacked it in 1858, the opening of the French conquest, and in 1888 the Nguyen court ceded it to France as a concession.

dadda-ii.s: Dadda II was a king of the Gurjara dynasty of Nandipuri, in southern Gujarat, in the first half of the 7th century. His copper-plate land grants are dated in the Kalachuri era, and later inscriptions of his family claim that he protected the Maitraka king of Valabhi when he…

dagobert-i.s: Dagobert I was a Merovingian king of the Franks, made king of Austrasia in 623 and ruler of all the Frankish kingdoms from 629 until his death in 639. With advisers such as Eligius he strengthened royal power, and he was a patron of the abbey of Saint-Denis, where he was the…

dahlak-kebir.s: Dahlak Kebir is the largest island of the Dahlak Archipelago in the Red Sea, off the coast of Eritrea near Massawa. From the 10th century it was the seat of a Muslim sultanate that controlled the sea approaches to the Ethiopian coast.

dalpat-shah.s: Dalpat Shah was a Gond king of Garha-Mandla in central India, the son of Sangram Shah. He married Durgavati, a princess of the Chandela line of Mahoba, and after his early death around 1550 she ruled as regent for their young son Vir Narayan.

dang-darbar.s: The Dang Darbar is an annual gathering at Ahwa in the Dangs district of Gujarat, India, held before Holi. Under British rule the chiefs of the Dang states, small Bhil chiefdoms of the forest, assembled there each year to receive payments for the forest leases they had granted.

daniel-coxe.s: Daniel Coxe was an English physician to Charles II and Queen Anne and a speculator in colonial land. In 1687 he bought the proprietary rights to West Jersey from the heirs of Edward Byllynge and styled himself governor, though he never visited the colony.

daniel-de-la-touche.s: Daniel de La Touche, seigneur de La Ravardière, was a French Protestant naval officer who explored the coasts of Guiana and northern Brazil. In 1612 he and François de Razilly founded the colony of Equinoctial France on the island of Maranhão, building the fort of Saint-Louis,…

daniel-ortega.s: Daniel Ortega is a Nicaraguan politician, a leader of the Sandinista National Liberation Front that overthrew the Somoza dictatorship in 1979. He headed the revolutionary junta and was president from 1985 to 1990, during the Contra war, before losing the 1990 election to…

daniele-manin.s: Daniele Manin was a Venetian lawyer and patriot who led the Republic of San Marco in 1848–1849. Freed from Austrian imprisonment by crowds in March 1848, he proclaimed the republic and as its president organised the city's defence.

danilo-i-metropolitan-of-cetinje.s: Danilo I was Metropolitan of Cetinje from 1697 and founder of the Petrović-Njegoš dynasty, which held the prince-bishopric of Montenegro by succession from uncle to nephew. He led the Montenegrin clans against Ottoman control, and in 1711 allied Montenegro with Peter the Great…

danilo-i-prince-of-montenegro.s: Danilo I was the ruler of Montenegro who in 1852 declined consecration as a bishop and made himself secular prince, turning the prince-bishopric into a hereditary principality with Russian backing. He issued a general law code in 1855, and his brother Mirko defeated the…

danish-east-india-company.s: The Danish East India Company was a trading company chartered by Christian IV in 1616 to trade with Asia. Its first expedition, under Ove Gjedde, obtained Tranquebar on the Coromandel coast from the Nayak of Thanjavur in 1620, where the fort of Dansborg was built.

daniyal-bek.s: Daniyal Bek was the last sultan of Elisu, a small Muslim principality on the southern slopes of the Greater Caucasus. Although a major general in Russian service, he joined Imam Shamil in 1844, and Russia abolished his sultanate.

darial-pass.s: The Darial Pass is a gorge of the Terek River through the central Greater Caucasus, on the border between Georgia and Russia. Since antiquity it has been the main route across the mountains, guarded by fortifications known to classical writers as the Caspian or Alan Gates.

date-hidemune.s: Date Hidemune was the eldest son of Date Masamune and the first lord of the Uwajima Domain on Shikoku. Born to a concubine and held for years as a hostage of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, he was passed over as heir to the Sendai Domain.

date-munenari.s: Date Munenari was lord of the Uwajima Domain from 1844 to 1858 and one of the 'four wise lords' of the late Edo period. He promoted Western learning, sheltering the scholar Takano Choei and employing Murata Zoroku, later Omura Masujiro, and had a steamship built by local…

date-tanemune.s: Date Tanemune was head of the Date clan in southern Mutsu in the early 16th century and the first of his family appointed military governor of Mutsu. In 1536 he issued the Jinkaishu, one of the most detailed regional law codes of the Sengoku period.

dato-mogol.s: Dato Mogol was a Muslim leader, said to be of Persian or Malay origin, who around 1605 founded a fortified port at Singora, present-day Songkhla, on the east coast of the Malay peninsula. Paying tribute to Ayutthaya, the settlement grew rich on trade with Dutch and English…

datu-uto.s: Datu Uto was the ruler of Buayan on the upper Pulangi River in Mindanao and the most powerful Maguindanao leader of the later 19th century. Exchanging captives and forest goods for firearms, he dominated the Cotabato valley as the Maguindanao sultanate weakened under Spanish…

daud-khan-karrani.s: Daud Khan Karrani was the last Afghan sultan of Bengal, of the Karrani dynasty, ruling from 1572. He provoked a war with Akbar by attacking a Mughal fort, lost Patna and Bihar in 1574 and submitted after the Battle of Tukaroi in 1575.

david-marshall.s: David Marshall was a Singaporean lawyer of Baghdadi Jewish descent who became the first chief minister of Singapore in 1955, after his Labour Front won the first elections under the Rendel Constitution. He resigned in 1956 when talks in London on self-government failed.

david-of-burgundy.s: David of Burgundy was an illegitimate son of Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, who had him made bishop of Utrecht in 1456 against the chapter's own candidate. Previously bishop of Thérouanne, he extended Burgundian influence over the northern Netherlands.

david-vi-narin.s: David VI Narin was king of Georgia, crowned as co-ruler with his cousin David VII Ulu under Mongol overlordship. In 1259 he rebelled against the Mongols and, after the rising failed, withdrew to Kutaisi, where he ruled western Georgia as a separate kingdom, the origin of the…

dawda-jawara.s: Dawda Jawara was a Gambian veterinarian and politician who led The Gambia to independence from Britain in 1965. His People's Progressive Party won the elections of 1962, making him head of government, and he became president when the country became a republic in 1970.

dawsonne-drake.s: Dawsonne Drake was an official of the British East India Company who served as governor of Manila during the British occupation of 1762–1764, after its capture in the Seven Years' War. His harsh rule and quarrels with the military commanders were later criticised by the company.

dayfa-khatun.s: Dayfa Khatun was an Ayyubid princess, daughter of al-Adil I and niece of Saladin, who married al-Zahir Ghazi, ruler of Aleppo. After the death of her son al-Aziz Muhammad in 1236 she governed Aleppo as regent for her grandson al-Nasir Yusuf until 1242, one of the few women to…

dead-sea.s: The Dead Sea is a salt lake in the Jordan Rift Valley between Jordan to the east and Israel and the West Bank to the west, its shore the lowest land on Earth. In antiquity the kingdom of Moab lay on the plateau east of it.

dean-barrow.s: Dean Barrow is a Belizean lawyer and politician, leader of the United Democratic Party, who was prime minister of Belize from 2008 to 2020. He had earlier served as foreign minister and deputy prime minister under Manuel Esquivel.

debre-libanos.s: Debre Libanos is a monastery in the Shewa highlands north of Addis Ababa, founded in the 13th century by the saint Tekle Haymanot. Its abbot, the echege, became the leading figure of Ethiopian monasticism.

decimus-junius-brutus-callaicus.s: Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus was a Roman general and consul in 138 BCE. Governing Hispania Ulterior, he campaigned against the Lusitanians after the death of Viriathus and in 137 BCE marched north across the Douro and Minho against the Callaeci, earning the surname Callaicus.

deiotarus.s: Deiotarus was a Galatian tetrarch who became king of Galatia in the 1st century BCE as a loyal ally of Rome. Pompey rewarded his help against Mithridates VI with lands including Lesser Armenia.

deiotarus-philadelphus.s: Deiotarus Philadelphus was the last king of Paphlagonia, a Roman client ruler in northern Anatolia. A son of Castor of Galatia and grandson of Deiotarus, he received Paphlagonia from Mark Antony and kept it under Augustus.

del-carretto.s: The Del Carretto were a Ligurian and Piedmontese noble family descended from the Aleramici marquises of Savona. From the 12th century they ruled the Marquisate of Finale and other fiefs on the western Riviera, with their seat at Finalborgo, while the port of Noli freed itself…

denes-berinkey.s: Dénes Berinkey was a Hungarian lawyer and politician who served as prime minister of the Hungarian Democratic Republic from January to March 1919, under President Mihály Károlyi. His government resigned on 21 March 1919, after the Allied Vix Note demanded a further Hungarian…

denzil-douglas.s: Denzil Douglas is a Kittitian physician and politician who led the Saint Kitts and Nevis Labour Party and was prime minister from 1995 to 2015, the longest tenure in the country's history. His government faced the 1998 referendum in which Nevis narrowly failed to secede, and…

derek-walcott.s: Derek Walcott was a Saint Lucian poet and playwright, born in Castries in 1930 when the island was a British colony. His work, including the epic poem Omeros (1990), drew on Caribbean history, landscape and mixed heritage, and he founded the Trinidad Theatre Workshop.

dervish-ali.s: Dervish Ali was the last khan of Astrakhan. He had briefly ruled before, and in 1554 the forces of Ivan IV installed him as a Russian client khan.

desi-bouterse.s: Desi Bouterse was a Surinamese soldier and politician who seized power in a coup in February 1980 and ruled as military strongman through the 1980s. His regime carried out the December murders of 1982, in which fifteen opponents were killed, and fought the Jungle Commando in…

desu-singh.s: Desu Singh was a Sikh chief of the Bhai family who seized Kaithal, in present-day Haryana, around 1767 during the Sikh expansion into the former Mughal province of Sirhind. He founded the state of Kaithal, which his descendants ruled until it lapsed to the British in 1843.

deutsche-mark.s: The Deutsche Mark was the currency of West Germany from June 1948 and of reunified Germany from 1990 until it was replaced by the euro in 2002. Its introduction in the western zones of occupied Germany helped end the black market and prompted the Soviet blockade of West Berlin.

dewa-agung-istri-kanya.s: Dewa Agung Istri Kanya was a queen of Klungkung, the senior kingdom of Bali, in the mid-19th century. During the Dutch expedition of 1849 she led the resistance at Kusamba, where the Dutch commander General Andreas Michiels was mortally wounded in a night attack.

dewa-agung-jambe-ii.s: Dewa Agung Jambe II was the last king of Klungkung, the senior royal house of Bali, from 1903. When the Dutch attacked in April 1908 he led his family and followers out of the palace in a puputan, a ritual suicidal march into rifle fire, in which he and around two hundred…

dhanya-manikya.s: Dhanya Manikya was king of Tripura from about 1490 to 1515 and one of the most powerful rulers of the Manikya dynasty. He expanded the kingdom into eastern Bengal and towards Chittagong, fighting the Bengal Sultanate under Alauddin Husain Shah.

dharmapala-pala-emperor.s: Dharmapala was the second ruler of the Pala Empire of Bengal and Bihar, reigning from about 770 to 810. He extended Pala power up the Ganges, installing his protégé Chakrayudha as king of Kannauj, and fought the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas for northern India.

dharmapala-of-kotte.s: Dharmapala of Kotte was the last king of Kotte in Sri Lanka, placed on the throne as a child in 1551 under Portuguese protection. Baptised as Dom João Dharmapala in 1557, he lost the support of most of his subjects to Mayadunne of Sitawaka.

dhimiter-progoni.s: Dhimitër Progoni was the ruler of Arbanon, the first recorded Albanian principality, from about 1208 to 1215, succeeding his brother Gjin. Styled panhypersebastos, he married Komnena, daughter of Stefan the First-Crowned of Serbia, and corresponded with Pope Innocent III about…

dhruvasena-ii.s: Dhruvasena II, also called Baladitya, was a king of the Maitraka dynasty of Valabhi in Gujarat in the early 7th century. Defeated by Harsha of Kannauj, he became his ally and married Harsha's daughter.

dhu-ghabat.s: Dhu Ghabat was the chief god of the oasis of Dedan, modern al-Ula in north-western Arabia, worshipped under the kingdoms of Dedan and Lihyan. Dadanitic inscriptions record offerings, vows and taxes paid at his sanctuaries, and his priests held an important place in the town.

dhu-raydan.s: Dhu Raydan, after Raydan, the royal palace at the Himyarite capital Zafar, was the name by which the Himyarite kingdom of south Arabia appears in its inscriptions. From the 1st century CE its kings used the title 'King of Saba and Dhu Raydan', claiming the old Sabaean crown.

diaba-lompo.s: Diaba Lompo is the legendary founder of the Gulmance kingdom of Gulmu, centred on Fada N'Gourma in eastern Burkina Faso. Tradition says he descended from the sky with his followers and established the ruling dynasty, usually placed between the 13th and 15th centuries.

dial-diop.s: Dial Diop was a Lebou Muslim leader of the Cape Verde peninsula, in present-day Senegal, who led the revolt against the kingdom of Cayor in the 1790s. After repelling Cayor's forces, the Lebou established an independent republic around 1795, with Dial Diop as its first serigne.

diarmait-mac-mael-na-mbo.s: Diarmait mac Máel na mBó was king of Leinster from about 1042 and one of the most powerful rulers in Ireland until his death in 1072. Of the Uí Chennselaig of south Leinster, he took Dublin in 1052, made his son Murchad its king and sheltered the sons of Harold Godwinson after…

diego-columbus.s: Diego Columbus was the eldest son of Christopher Columbus and governor of the Indies at Santo Domingo from 1509. Pursuing his father's hereditary claims against the Spanish crown, he won recognition as admiral and viceroy, sent Juan de Esquivel to settle Jamaica in 1509 and…

diego-de-almagro.s: Diego de Almagro was a Spanish conquistador and partner of Francisco Pizarro in the conquest of Peru. In 1534 Charles V granted him the Governorate of New Toledo south of Pizarro's lands, and he led the first Spanish expedition into Chile in 1535–1537.

diego-de-almagro-the-younger.s: Diego de Almagro the Younger was the son of the conquistador Diego de Almagro and an Indigenous woman of Panama. Leading his father's followers, he had Francisco Pizarro killed in Lima in June 1541 and proclaimed himself governor of Peru.

diego-de-losada.s: Diego de Losada was a Spanish conquistador who founded Santiago de León de Caracas in 1567, after campaigning against the Indigenous peoples of the valley. Born in the kingdom of León, he had served in Venezuela for many years.

diego-de-montemayor.s: Diego de Montemayor was a Spanish settler and official who founded the city of Monterrey on 20 September 1596. A lieutenant of Luis de Carvajal y de la Cueva in the New Kingdom of León, he took over the colony after Carvajal's arrest by the Inquisition and refounded its…

diego-de-vargas.s: Diego de Vargas was a Spanish governor of New Mexico who led its reconquest after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680. In 1692 he reoccupied Santa Fe largely without bloodshed, and in 1693 he returned with settlers, retaking the city by force when its Pueblo occupants resisted.

diego-portales.s: Diego Portales was a Chilean merchant and minister who dominated the conservative governments of the 1830s. He imposed order on a divided country and shaped the centralist Constitution of 1833, which created a strong presidency.

diego-velazquez-de-cuellar.s: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar was a Spanish conquistador who led the conquest of Cuba from 1511 and became its first governor. He founded Baracoa, Santiago de Cuba and Havana, and the Taíno chief Hatuey, who resisted, was burnt in 1512.

diet-of-schwabisch-hall.s: The Diet of Schwäbisch Hall was an imperial assembly held in 1190 at Schwäbisch Hall in Swabia under King Henry VI. It ruled that the ducal authority of Henry I of Louvain applied only to his own lands, reducing the old duchy of Lower Lotharingia to a title.

dietrich-klagges.s: Dietrich Klagges was a German Nazi politician who served as interior minister of the Free State of Brunswick from 1931 and as its minister-president from 1933 to 1945. In February 1932 he appointed Adolf Hitler to a post in Brunswick's legation in Berlin, giving the stateless…

dietrich-of-haldensleben.s: Dietrich of Haldensleben was a Saxon count who became the first margrave of the Northern March in 965, ruling lands east of the Elbe over the Hevelli and Lutician Slavs. His harsh rule contributed to the Great Slav Rising of 983, in which the Slavs destroyed Brandenburg and…

digvijaysinhji.s: Digvijaysinhji was the Jam Sahib of Nawanagar from 1933, nephew and successor of the cricketer Ranjitsinhji. During the Second World War he gave refuge to hundreds of Polish children at Balachadi.

dinh-phe-de.s: Dinh Phe De, born Dinh Toan, was the second and last emperor of the Dinh dynasty in Vietnam, put on the throne as a child after his father Dinh Tien Hoang was murdered in 979. Facing a Song invasion, the court and his mother made the general Le Hoan emperor in 980, founding…

dinmukhamed-kunaev.s: Dinmukhamed Kunaev was a Kazakh Communist leader who headed the Communist Party of the Kazakh SSR from 1960 to 1962 and again from 1964 to 1986, and sat on the Soviet Politburo. A close ally of Leonid Brezhnev, he oversaw the growth of Almaty and of industry in the republic.

demetrius-the-fair.s: Demetrius the Fair was a Macedonian prince, son of Demetrius I Poliorcetes and half-brother of Antigonus II Gonatas. After the death of Magas of Cyrene around 250 BCE, the widowed queen Apama invited him to marry her daughter Berenice and rule Cyrene, undoing Magas's plan to…

demetrius-zvonimir.s: Demetrius Zvonimir was king of Croatia from 1076 to 1089, having earlier been ban of Slavonia. He was crowned at Solin in 1076 by a legate of Pope Gregory VII, swearing loyalty to the papacy.

democratic-labour-party-barbados.s: The Democratic Labour Party is a political party of Barbados, founded in 1955 by Errol Barrow and other dissidents from Grantley Adams's Barbados Labour Party. It won the 1961 elections, and under Barrow led Barbados to independence on 30 November 1966.

diogo-de-azambuja.s: Diogo de Azambuja was a Portuguese captain and nobleman sent by King John II to the Gold Coast. In 1482, after negotiating with a local ruler remembered as Caramansa, he built the fortress of São Jorge da Mina at Elmina, the first permanent European stronghold in sub-Saharan…

dionisio-de-herrera.s: Dionisio de Herrera was a Honduran liberal lawyer and politician who became the first head of state of Honduras within the Federal Republic of Central America, serving from 1824 to 1827. He oversaw the state's first constitution of 1825, with Comayagua as capital, before…

dionysius-ii-of-syracuse.s: Dionysius II of Syracuse, called the Younger, succeeded his father Dionysius I as tyrant of Syracuse in 367 BCE. Driven out by his kinsman Dion in 357, he took refuge in Locri Epizephyrii, his mother's city, and ruled it harshly until about 346, when he regained Syracuse.

dirk-iii-count-of-holland.s: Dirk III, Count of Holland, ruled the West Frisian county that later became Holland from 993. He seized the marshy lands around the Merwede and levied tolls on Rhine shipping, and in 1018 his forces defeated an imperial army sent against him at the Battle of Vlaardingen.

diviciacus-aedui.s: Diviciacus was a druid and leading noble of the Aedui of central Gaul and the only druid known by name from antiquity. Around 61 BCE he pleaded before the Roman Senate for help against the Sequani and Ariovistus, and he later supported Julius Caesar during the Gallic Wars,…

diviciacus-suessiones.s: Diviciacus was a king of the Suessiones of northern Gaul whom Julius Caesar was told had, within living memory, been the most powerful ruler in Gaul. His authority reportedly extended over much of Belgic Gaul and into Britain.

diyar-bakr.s: Diyar Bakr was the medieval Arabic name for the northernmost province of the Jazira, the upper Tigris basin around Amid (modern Diyarbakır) and Mayyafariqin. Named after the Arab tribe of Bakr ibn Wa'il, it was contested by Byzantines, Hamdanids and Buyids before the Kurdish…

djoumbe-fatima.s: Djoumbe Fatima was queen of Mohéli in the Comoros, succeeding her father Ramanetaka, a Merina prince, as a child in 1842. Her reign was marked by rivalry between French and British interests, and she abdicated in favour of her son in 1867, returning to power for a time later.

dmitry-of-suzdal.s: Dmitry of Suzdal, Dmitry Konstantinovich, was prince of Suzdal and Nizhny Novgorod and held the Golden Horde's patent as Grand Prince of Vladimir from 1360 to 1363. Moscow's young Dmitry Donskoy then displaced him, and he made peace by marrying his daughter Evdokia to Dmitry.

dmitry-korybut.s: Dmitry Korybut was a Lithuanian prince of the Gediminid dynasty, a son of Grand Duke Algirdas, who held Novgorod-Seversky in the late 14th century. He was baptised in the Orthodox faith and took part in the dynastic struggles of his brothers Jogaila and Vytautas, sometimes in…

dmitry-ulyanov.s: Dmitry Ulyanov was a Bolshevik physician and the youngest brother of Vladimir Lenin. In spring 1919 he became deputy chairman and effective head of the council of people's commissars of the short-lived Crimean Socialist Soviet Republic, which collapsed before the White advance…

dobrica-cosic.s: Dobrica Ćosić was a Serbian novelist and political figure whose works on Serbia's wars made him a leading voice of Serbian nationalism. In 1992 he became the first president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, formed by Serbia and Montenegro.

dobromir-chrysos.s: Dobromir Chrysos was a Vlach or Bulgarian commander who served in the Byzantine army and broke away during the Asen revolt that created the Second Bulgarian Empire. From the fortress of Prosek in the Vardar gorge he ruled an independent lordship in Macedonia, fought off…

dodda-vira-rajendra.s: Dodda Vira Rajendra was raja of Coorg in the Western Ghats. Held captive by Tipu Sultan of Mysore, he escaped in 1788, regained his kingdom and allied with the British East India Company against Mysore in the Anglo-Mysore wars.

dodo-soomro.s: Dodo Soomro was a ruler of the Soomra dynasty of Sindh remembered in Sindhi folk poetry and legend for resisting the armies of the Delhi Sultanate. His story, often linked with his brother Chanesar in the tale of Dodo and Chanesar, celebrates defence of Sindh and its honour.

dolon-nor.s: Dolon Nor, now Duolun in Inner Mongolia, is a town on the steppe north of Beijing. In 1691 the Kangxi Emperor held a great assembly there at which the Khalkha Mongol princes, driven south by the Dzungar ruler Galdan, formally submitted to the Qing dynasty.

domesday-book.s: Domesday Book is the record of the great survey of England ordered by William the Conqueror in 1085 and largely completed in 1086. It lists landholders, manors, resources and taxable values across most of the kingdom, giving an unmatched picture of the land after the Norman…

domingo-martinez-de-irala.s: Domingo Martínez de Irala was a Basque conquistador who came to the Río de la Plata with Pedro de Mendoza and became the dominant figure of early Paraguay. Elected governor by the settlers of Asunción, he deposed Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca in 1544 and ruled the colony for most…

domingos-jose-martins.s: Domingos José Martins was a Brazilian merchant and one of the leaders of the Pernambucan Revolt of 1817 against Portuguese rule. As a member of the provisional government of the Republic of Pernambuco he helped abolish some taxes and proclaim freedom of conscience and the press.

domnall-mor-ua-briain.s: Domnall Mór Ua Briain was king of Thomond and, at times, of Munster from 1168. He submitted to Henry II of England in 1171 but fought the Anglo-Normans for much of his reign, defeating them at Thurles in 1174.

donal-maccarthy-mor-1st-earl-of-clancare.n: Donal MacCarthy Mór, 1st Earl of Clancare
donal-maccarthy-mor-1st-earl-of-clancare.s: Donal MacCarthy Mór was the last MacCarthy Mór, head of the MacCarthy dynasty of Desmond in south-west Ireland. Under the Tudor policy of surrender and regrant he was created Earl of Clancare in 1565, but he twice rebelled against the Crown.

donal-an-chogaidh-o-flaithbheartaigh.s: Dónal an Chogaidh Ó Flaithbheartaigh, 'Donal of the Battles', was a chieftain of the O'Flaherty lordship of Iar Connacht in western Ireland and heir to its leadership. He was the first husband of the sea captain Grace O'Malley, with whom he had three children.

donn-carrach-maguire.s: Donn Carrach Maguire is counted as the first Maguire king of Fermanagh, ruling from about 1264 until his death in 1302. His accession marked the rise of the Maguires over older lineages in the lakeland of Fermanagh, and his descendants ruled the territory until the Plantation…

donnchad-ua-cerbaill.s: Donnchad Ua Cerbaill was king of Airgialla in the north of Ireland in the 12th century. He extended his realm into Louth and was a major supporter of church reform, founding Mellifont Abbey in 1142 with St Malachy, the first Cistercian monastery in Ireland.

donyo-dorje.s: Donyö Dorje was the most powerful ruler of the Rinpungpa dynasty of Tsang in central Tibet. Around 1498 his forces took control of the Lhasa region, and as patron of the Karma Kagyu school he barred Gelug monks from Lhasa's Great Prayer Festival until 1517.

dorde-stratimirovic.s: Đorđe Stratimirović was a Serbian officer from the Habsburg monarchy who led the armed forces and the Main Board of the Serbian Vojvodina during the revolution of 1848–1849. He organised Serb resistance to the Hungarian government in Srem, Bačka and Banat, but quarrelled with…

douglas-macarthur.s: Douglas MacArthur was an American general who served as military adviser to the Commonwealth of the Philippines from 1935 and commanded Allied forces in the South-West Pacific during the Second World War. As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers he directed the occupation of…

drakpa-gyaltsen-phagmodrupa.s: Drakpa Gyaltsen was ruler of central Tibet from the Phagmodrupa dynasty, reigning from 1385 to 1432, the high point of the dynasty's power. His long, peaceful reign saw strong government from Nedong and close ties with the Ming court.

duan-kan.s: Duan Kan was a chief of the Duan Xianbei who, after the Duan were broken by Former Yan, held the area around Guanggu in Shandong as a semi-independent ruler in the mid-4th century. He alternated nominal allegiance between Eastern Jin and other powers until Former Yan besieged…

duan-pidi.s: Duan Pidi was a chief of the Duan Xianbei in north China in the early 4th century, nominally loyal to the Jin dynasty. In 318 he killed the Jin loyalist general Liu Kun, who had sought refuge with him, an act widely condemned.

duan-qirui.s: Duan Qirui was a Chinese general and politician, a protégé of Yuan Shikai and leader of the Anhui clique of the Beiyang Army. He served several times as premier of the Beiyang government in Beijing, brought China into the First World War in 1917 and took large Japanese loans.

duan-xingzhi.s: Duan Xingzhi was the last king of the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan. When a Mongol army under Kublai took the capital Dali in 1253, he fled but was captured in 1254.

duarte-coelho.s: Duarte Coelho was a Portuguese soldier and navigator who had served in Asia before King John III granted him the captaincy of Pernambuco in 1534. Calling it Nova Lusitânia, he founded Olinda and built a colony based on sugar mills, which became the most prosperous of the…

duchy-of-saxe-coburg.s: The Duchy of Saxe-Coburg was an Ernestine Saxon duchy centred on Coburg in Franconia. It first existed under Duke John Casimir until 1633, and was revived in 1680 when the lands of Ernest the Pious were divided among his sons.

duke-gong-of-cao.s: Duke Gong of Cao ruled the small Zhou state of Cao in the 7th century BCE. He is remembered for slighting the exiled Prince Chong'er of Jin, spying on him in his bath to see his reputedly joined ribs.

duke-hu-of-chen.s: Duke Hu of Chen, Gui Man, was the founder of the State of Chen. King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed him at Wanqiu, modern Huaiyang in Henan, as a descendant of the legendary Emperor Shun, so that sacrifices to Shun could continue, and gave him his eldest daughter in marriage.

duke-hui-of-eastern-zhou.s: Duke Hui of Eastern Zhou, named Gen, was the founder of the Duchy of Eastern Zhou.
