didessa-river.s: The Didessa is a river in western Ethiopia and a major tributary of the Abay, the Blue Nile. In the 19th century its upper valley was home to the Oromo kingdoms of Gomma, Gumma and Limmu-Ennarea, whose wealth came from coffee, gold and trade.

dafydd-ap-gruffydd.s: Dafydd ap Gruffydd was a Welsh prince, brother of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, who repeatedly changed sides between his brother and Edward I of England. His attack on Hawarden Castle in March 1282 began the war that ended Welsh independence.

dhofar.s: Dhofar is the southern governorate of Oman, bordering Yemen, with its capital at Salalah. Its monsoon-watered hills are the classic home of frankincense, traded since antiquity through ports such as Sumhuram (Khor Rori).

danish-icelandic-act-of-union.s: The Danish–Icelandic Act of Union was an agreement between Denmark and Iceland that took effect on 1 December 1918, recognising Iceland as a fully sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark under King Christian X. Denmark handled Iceland's foreign affairs on its behalf,…

dublin-castle.s: Dublin Castle is a complex of buildings in central Dublin, begun in the early 13th century on the orders of King John. For about 700 years it was the seat of English and later British government in Ireland, housing the lord deputy or lord lieutenant and the administration, so…

dzibanche.s: Dzibanche is a Maya archaeological site in southern Quintana Roo, Mexico, occupied from the late Preclassic period. Inscriptions show that it was the seat of the Kaan, or snake-head, dynasty in the 5th and 6th centuries CE, before the dynasty moved to Calakmul in the 7th century.

dantapura.s: Dantapura was an ancient city named in Buddhist and Jain texts and in the Mahabharata as a capital of Kalinga on India's east coast. According to Buddhist tradition, the tooth relic of the Buddha was kept there before it was taken to Sri Lanka in the 4th century CE.

dala-hill.s: Dala Hill is a rocky hill inside the old city of Kano in northern Nigeria. According to the Kano Chronicle, its iron ore and the cult of a local spirit drew the first settlers, and Kano's earliest communities lived around it before the city walls were built.

david-oates.s: David Oates was a British archaeologist of ancient Mesopotamia. He worked with Max Mallowan at Nimrud, directed the excavations at Tell al-Rimah in northern Iraq in the 1960s, and with his wife Joan Oates led the long-running excavations at Tell Brak in Syria from 1976.

djurdjura.s: The Djurdjura is a mountain range of the Tell Atlas in northern Algeria, rising to 2,308 m at Lalla Khedidja and forming the backbone of Greater Kabylia. Its villages were the base of the Kabyle kingdom of Kuku in the 16th and 17th centuries and long resisted outside rule,…

dosunmu.s: Dosunmu, also spelt Docemo, was Oba of Lagos from 1853 to 1885, succeeding his father Akitoye. Under strong pressure from the British consul and a naval squadron, he signed the treaty of 6 August 1861 ceding Lagos to Britain in return for a pension, and Lagos became a British…

danes.s: The Danes are the North Germanic people of Denmark. In the Viking Age Danish armies raided and conquered much of England and settled the Danelaw, and from the 12th century the Danish kingdom expanded into the Baltic, ruling northern Estonia until 1346.

daumantas-of-pskov.s: Daumantas of Pskov was a Lithuanian prince who took part in the murder of King Mindaugas in 1263 and then fled to Pskov. Baptised as Timothy, he ruled Pskov as its prince from 1266 until his death in 1299 and defended it against the Livonian Order.

durrow-abbey.s: Durrow Abbey was a monastery near Tullamore in County Offaly, Ireland, founded by Columba around 553. It was one of the leading monasteries of early medieval Ireland and gave its name to the Book of Durrow, a 7th-century illuminated gospel book now in Trinity College Dublin.

donnchad-mac-gilla-patraic.s: Donnchad mac Gilla Pátraic was king of Osraige from 1003 and King of Leinster from 1033 until his death in 1039. A descendant of Cerball mac Dúnlainge, he was the ancestor of the Mac Giolla Phádraig (Fitzpatrick) family.

datames.s: Datames was a Carian-born Persian satrap of Cappadocia and one of the ablest generals of the Achaemenid Empire in the 4th century BCE. He captured the rebellious Paphlagonian ruler Thys and fought for Artaxerxes II, but later revolted against him, taking part in the Great…

dionysus.s: Dionysus was the Greek god of wine, vegetation, ecstasy and theatre, called Bacchus by the Romans. His name already appears on Linear B tablets of the Mycenaean age.

deganwy.s: Deganwy is a site on twin volcanic hills above the estuary of the River Conwy in north Wales, beside the modern town of the same name. Tradition links its early medieval fortress with Maelgwn Gwynedd, and excavation has found imported Mediterranean pottery of the 5th and 6th…

denbigh.s: Denbigh is a market town in north-east Wales, above the Vale of Clwyd, in the medieval cantref of Rhufoniog. A Welsh stronghold there was held by Dafydd ap Gruffudd before the English conquest, after which Henry de Lacy, Earl of Lincoln, built Denbigh Castle and a walled town…

debre-berhan.s: Debre Berhan is a town in the highlands of North Shewa, Ethiopia, north-east of Addis Ababa. It was founded by Emperor Zara Yaqob in the 1450s after a miraculous light was said to have appeared there, and served as his capital.

diakhao.s: Diakhao is a village in the Fatick Region of western Senegal that served as the royal capital of the Serer kingdom of Sine. The kings, titled Maad a Sinig, resided there with their court and great chiefs.

dakovo.s: Đakovo is a town in the Slavonia region of eastern Croatia, seat of a Catholic bishopric since the 13th century. Its large neo-Romanesque cathedral of St Peter was built between 1866 and 1882 under Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer.

dipavamsa.s: The Dipavamsa, the "Chronicle of the Island", is the oldest surviving historical chronicle of Sri Lanka, written in Pali probably in the 4th century CE. It recounts the legendary visits of the Buddha to the island, the arrival of Prince Vijaya and the history of its kings and…

dihya.s: Dihya, called al-Kahina, the prophetess, by Arab writers, was a Berber queen and war leader of the Aurès mountains in the late 7th century. Heading the Jarawa tribe, she defeated the Umayyad general Hassan ibn al-Nu'man in the 690s and held much of Ifriqiya for several years.

david-iii-kuropalates.s: David III Kuropalates was a Bagratid prince of Tao in south-western Georgia from the 960s until his death in 1001. He helped Emperor Basil II defeat the rebel Bardas Skleros in 979 and was rewarded with large territories, and he built churches such as Oshki.

diuma.s: Diuma was an Irish priest, one of four sent from Northumbria with Peada in 653 to preach to the Middle Angles. After Penda's death he was consecrated by Bishop Finan as the first bishop of the Mercians and Middle Angles, a see covering the whole Mercian kingdom.

djedars.s: The Djedars are thirteen stepped pyramid-shaped mausoleums on hilltops near Frenda and Tiaret in north-western Algeria, built between the 5th and 7th centuries. Standing on square bases with internal chambers, they are attributed to Berber kings who ruled the region after the…

donegal-castle.s: Donegal Castle stands on the River Eske in Donegal town, Ireland. The O'Donnell lords of Tír Chonaill built its tower house in 1474 as their main seat.

donegal-friary.s: Donegal Friary was a Franciscan house founded in 1474 by Hugh Roe O'Donnell, lord of Tír Chonaill, and his wife Nuala at Donegal town. It was the family's chief religious foundation and burial place.

dungannon.s: Dungannon is a town in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland. It was the chief seat of the O'Neill kings of Tír Eoghain from the late Middle Ages, with their inauguration site at nearby Tullyhogue, and Hugh O'Neill ruled from its castle.

daingean.s: Daingean is a village in County Offaly in the Irish midlands, once the chief stronghold of the O'Connor Faly lords. After the English took it in the 1540s, it was renamed Philipstown in 1556 after Philip II, husband of Mary I, and became the county town of the new King's County.

drusus-the-younger.s: Drusus the Younger was the son of the Roman emperor Tiberius and his intended heir. In 17–20 CE he commanded in Illyricum, where he exploited the quarrels of the Germanic peoples and settled the followers of the Marcomannic king Maroboduus beyond the Danube under Vannius of…

danelaw.s: The Danelaw was the part of England settled and ruled by Scandinavians in the late 9th and 10th centuries, north and east of a line roughly along Watling Street. It took shape after the Great Heathen Army settled Northumbria, East Anglia and eastern Mercia, and its boundary…

dangbe.s: Dangbe is the python deity of Ouidah, on the coast of Benin, honoured since the time of the kingdom of Hueda, or Whydah. Royal pythons were sacred in the town and could not be harmed, and European visitors of the 17th and 18th centuries described the cult and its priestesses.

dinefwr-castle.s: Dinefwr Castle stands on a ridge above the river Tywi near Llandeilo in Carmarthenshire, Wales. Welsh tradition made Dinefwr the chief seat of the kings of Deheubarth, and the stone castle was built by the Lord Rhys or his sons in the 12th and 13th centuries.

dharwad.s: Dharwad is a city in northern Karnataka, India, forming a twin city with Hubballi. Its fort was held by the Adil Shahis of Bijapur, the Mughals, the Marathas and Mysore before the British took the region in 1818.

dayak-people.s: The Dayak are the indigenous, mainly non-Malay peoples of the interior of Borneo, comprising many groups such as the Iban, Ngaju, Kayan and Kenyah. Traditionally they lived in longhouse communities along the rivers, practising shifting rice cultivation and, in some groups,…

dalian.s: Dalian is a port city in Liaoning province, China, near the southern tip of the Liaodong peninsula. Russia founded it in 1898 as the commercial port of Dalny within its Kwantung lease, and after 1905 Japan developed it as Dairen, headquarters of the South Manchuria Railway…

darangen.s: The Darangen is the epic of the Maranao people of the Lake Lanao region on Mindanao in the Philippines. Its long cycles of chanted verse tell of the hero Bantugan and other heroes, preserving Maranao history, customary law, values and aesthetics.

dang-tat.s: Đặng Tất was a Vietnamese general who joined the resistance against the Ming occupation after 1407. With Nguyen Canh Chan he led the Later Tran army of Emperor Gian Dinh to victory over the Ming at Bo Co in 1408.

dingzhou.s: Dingzhou is a city in Hebei province, northern China, south-west of Beijing. As Zhongshan it was an important city from the Warring States period and served as the capital of the Later Yan dynasty of Murong Chui in the late 4th century.

diana-mythology.s: Diana was the Roman goddess of hunting, wild animals, the moon and childbirth, later identified with the Greek Artemis. She was a federal goddess of the Latin peoples, worshipped in a sacred grove at Aricia beside Lake Nemi, and King Servius Tullius was said to have founded…

daugavpils.s: Daugavpils is the second largest city of Latvia, on the Daugava river in the south-eastern region of Latgale. Founded by the Livonian Order as Dünaburg in the 13th century, it later belonged to Poland-Lithuania and the Russian Empire, as Dvinsk.

damaras.s: The Damaras were a class of landholding gentry in medieval Kashmir who rose to power in the 11th and 12th centuries, controlling rural estates and armed retainers. Their rebellions and feuds with the kings of the Lohara dynasty, described at length in Kalhana's Rajatarangini,…

diego-lopez-v-de-haro.s: Diego López V de Haro was lord of Biscay and one of the leading nobles of the Crown of Castile, a member of the powerful Haro family. In 1300 he granted a town charter to Bilbao, founding the city that became Biscay's chief port.

dejan-sebastokrator.s: Dejan was a Serbian magnate of the 14th century who married Teodora, a sister of Stefan Dušan, and received the rank of sebastokrator. He held lands around Kumanovo and in the upper Struma valley.

dundrennan-abbey.s: Dundrennan Abbey is a ruined Cistercian abbey near Kirkcudbright in Galloway, south-west Scotland, founded in 1142 by Fergus of Galloway, perhaps with King David I, and settled by monks from Rievaulx. Mary, Queen of Scots spent her last night in Scotland there in May 1568…

despenser-family.s: The Despensers were an English noble family. Hugh Despenser the Younger, a favourite of Edward II, gained the lordship of Glamorgan through his marriage to Eleanor de Clare, a co-heiress of the Clare earls of Gloucester, and he and his father dominated the government until…

djerba.s: Djerba is an island in the Gulf of Gabès off southern Tunisia, the largest in North Africa. Long a trading and fishing centre, it has an ancient Jewish community and an Ibadi Muslim population.

duke-of-atholl.s: Duke of Atholl is a title in the peerage of Scotland created in 1703 for John Murray, Marquess of Atholl. In 1736 the 2nd Duke inherited the lordship of the Isle of Man from the Stanley earls of Derby through his grandmother, and the dukes held it until they sold their…

doberan-abbey.s: Doberan Abbey was a Cistercian monastery near the Baltic coast of Mecklenburg, founded in 1171 by Pribislav, the first Christian prince of the Obotrites. Its brick Gothic church, Doberan Minster, became the burial place of the Mecklenburg dynasty.

durad-i-balsic.s: Đurađ I Balšić was lord of Zeta, roughly modern Montenegro, from 1362 to 1378, the most capable of the three Balšić brothers who made Zeta independent as the Serbian Empire broke up. He fought rival lords such as Nikola Altomanović and gained part of his lands after Nikola's…

devotio-moderna.s: The Devotio Moderna was a religious reform movement founded by Geert Groote of Deventer in the late 14th century. It stressed inner piety, meditation and humble work, and spread through the Brethren of the Common Life and the canons of Windesheim across the Low Countries and…

da-polenta-family.s: The da Polenta were a family that ruled Ravenna from 1275 to 1441, and at times Cervia and other towns of Romagna. Their founder, Guido da Polenta the Elder, was the father of Francesca da Rimini; his grandson Guido Novello sheltered the exiled Dante, who died in Ravenna in 1321.

donald-lord-of-the-isles.s: Donald, Lord of the Isles, was the head of Clan Donald and ruler of the Hebrides and western Highlands from the late 1380s. Son of John of Islay and Margaret Stewart, daughter of King Robert II, he claimed the earldom of Ross through his wife Mariota.

dorieus.s: Dorieus was a Spartan prince, a son of King Anaxandridas II and half-brother of Cleomenes I. Passed over for the throne, he left Sparta around 515 BCE to found a colony on the Cinyps in Libya, but was expelled by the Macae and Carthaginians.

dumyat.s: Dumyat is a hill of 418 metres at the western end of the Ochil Hills, overlooking Stirling in central Scotland. Its name, from Gaelic Dùn Mhèadaidh, 'fort of the Maeatae', is thought to preserve the name of the Iron Age people who lived around the Forth valley in Roman times.

damkina.s: Damkina, also called Damgalnuna, was a Mesopotamian mother goddess, the wife of the god Ea (Enki), lord of fresh water and wisdom. In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish she is the mother of Marduk.

dilawar-khan-ghuri.s: Dilawar Khan Ghuri was the founder of the Malwa Sultanate in central India. Appointed governor of Malwa by the Tughlaq sultans in 1392, he ruled independently after Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 and took royal state around 1401, ruling from Dhar.

durlach.s: Durlach is a historic town in Baden-Württemberg, part of the city of Karlsruhe since 1938. It was the residence of the Protestant margraves of Baden-Durlach from 1565, who built the Karlsburg palace there.

dresden.s: Dresden is the capital of the German state of Saxony, on the Elbe. Residence of the Wettin rulers from the late 15th century, it became a Baroque capital under Augustus the Strong, with buildings such as the Zwinger and the Frauenkirche, and famous art collections.

damavand.s: Damavand is a town and district in the central Alborz mountains of northern Iran, east of Tehran, at the foot of Mount Damavand. In the early Islamic period it was ruled by the Masmughans, local lords of Iranian descent, until the Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan in 759–760.

da-cruz-family.s: The Da Cruz family were an Afro-Portuguese dynasty of prazo holders on the Zambezi in Mozambique. From their fortified base at Massangano, above Tete, they commanded Chikunda soldiers, taxed river trade and raided for slaves and ivory.

dubays-ibn-sadaqa.s: Dubays ibn Sadaqa was the Mazyadid emir of al-Hilla in Iraq from 1108 to 1135, son of Sadaqa ibn Mansur. A powerful Arab chief, he repeatedly fought the Abbasid caliphs and the Seljuk sultans, allied with Zengi and other rivals of the caliphs, and lost and regained Hilla…

dharmawangsa.s: Dharmawangsa Teguh was king of the Medang kingdom in East Java from about 990 to 1016. Around 990 he attacked Srivijaya in Sumatra without lasting success.

debarwa.s: Debarwa is a town in the central highlands of Eritrea, south of Asmara, near the Mareb river. From the fifteenth century it was the seat of the Bahr Negash, the governor of Medri Bahri under the Ethiopian emperors.

dzhengutai.s: Dzhengutai is a village in the Buynaksky district of Dagestan, in Russia's North Caucasus, in the foothills between the Kumyk plain and the Avar mountains. From around the seventeenth century it was the seat of the Mekhtuli Khanate, whose khans ruled the surrounding villages…

davit-bek.s: Davit Bek was an Armenian military leader who led a revolt in Syunik, in southern Armenia, from 1722, first against Persian khans and then against Ottoman invaders, as Safavid power collapsed. Backed by local meliks and in contact with Georgia and Russia, he won several…

dizak.s: Dizak was one of the five Armenian melikdoms of Karabakh, known as the Khamsa, in the south of the region. Ruled by the Melik-Avanian family, descended from Avan Yuzbashi, it kept its autonomy under the Safavids and Nader Shah but was subordinated to the Karabakh Khanate in…

de-administrando-imperio.s: De Administrando Imperio is a Greek handbook on foreign policy compiled around 950 by the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos for his son Romanos. It describes the peoples around the empire, such as the Pechenegs, Rus', Croats, Serbs and Hungarians, and advises…

demchugdongrub.s: Demchugdongrub, known as Prince De (De Wang), was an Inner Mongolian prince who led a movement for Mongol autonomy from China in the 1930s. Turning to Japan for support, he headed the Mongol Military Government from 1936 and the collaborationist Mengjiang government at Kalgan.

dai-nihonshi.s: The Dai Nihonshi, 'Great History of Japan', is a history of Japan in classical Chinese begun in 1657 by Tokugawa Mitsukuni, lord of the Mito domain, and completed only in 1906. Modelled on Chinese dynastic histories, it covers the emperors from Jimmu to the 14th century, and…

dhiban.s: Dhiban, biblical Dibon, is a town in Jordan east of the Dead Sea and north of the Arnon gorge. In the 9th century BCE it was the capital of the kingdom of Moab under King Mesha, who recorded his building works there.

danzantes.s: The Danzantes, 'dancers', are some three hundred carved stone slabs at Monte Albán in Oaxaca, Mexico, made in the city's earliest period, about 500 to 200 BCE. They show naked men in contorted poses, once thought to be dancers but now generally interpreted as slain or…

democratic-party-of-socialists-of-monten.n: Democratic Party of Socialists of Montenegro
democratic-party-of-socialists-of-monten.s: The Democratic Party of Socialists of Montenegro is a political party founded in 1991 as the successor of the League of Communists of Montenegro. Led for most of its history by Milo Đukanović, it governed Montenegro without interruption for three decades, first within…

deir-al-qamar.s: Deir al-Qamar is a town in the Chouf mountains of Lebanon, south-east of Beirut. It was the seat of the Ma'n and Shihab emirs of Mount Lebanon until Bashir II moved his court to nearby Beiteddine, and it preserves the palace of Fakhr al-Din II.

druze.s: The Druze are an Arabic-speaking religious community whose faith arose from Ismaili Islam in Egypt in the early 11th century, around the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim. Closed to converts since the mid-11th century, they live mainly in the mountains of Lebanon, Syria and northern…

djemal-pasha.s: Djemal Pasha was an Ottoman officer and politician, one of the three Young Turk leaders who governed the empire during the First World War. As commander in Syria from 1914 he led failed attacks on the Suez Canal, abolished the autonomy of Mount Lebanon and executed Arab…

daulat-qazi.s: Daulat Qazi was a Bengali poet of the early 17th century who wrote at the court of Mrauk U in Arakan, under the patronage of the minister Ashraf Khan. His romance Sati Mayna o Lor Chandrani, left unfinished at his death and completed by Alaol, is among the first Bengali poems…

dingiswayo.s: Dingiswayo was the paramount chief of the Mthethwa in present-day KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, from about 1795 until 1818. He organised young men into age-based regiments and extended his authority over many neighbouring chiefdoms, among them the Zulu, whose young leader Shaka…

demetrias.s: Demetrias was a Greek city on the Pagasetic Gulf in Thessaly, near modern Volos, founded by Demetrius Poliorcetes around 293 BCE by merging the populations of nearby towns. With Chalcis and Corinth it was one of the 'fetters of Greece', the fortresses through which the…

drigung-kagyu.s: The Drigung Kagyu is a school of the Kagyu tradition of Tibetan Buddhism, founded by Jigten Sumgön, who established Drigung Thil monastery north-east of Lhasa in 1179. In the 13th century it was a major religious and political power in central Tibet until its defeat by the…

drukpa-kagyu.s: The Drukpa Kagyu, or Drukpa lineage, is a school of the Kagyu tradition of Tibetan Buddhism founded in the late 12th century by Tsangpa Gyare, named after the Druk monastery he founded near Lhasa. In the 17th century the Drukpa lama Ngawang Namgyal fled to Bhutan and unified…

durban.s: Durban is the largest city of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, and one of Africa's busiest ports, on the Indian Ocean coast. British traders founded Port Natal there in 1824, and it was renamed in 1835 after Sir Benjamin D'Urban, governor of the Cape Colony.

dick-king.s: Dick King was an English-born settler in Natal, famous for his ride in 1842 to bring help to the British garrison besieged by the Boers at Port Natal after the Battle of Congella. With his servant Ndongeni he covered about 960 km to Grahamstown in ten days.

dilma-rousseff.s: Dilma Rousseff is a Brazilian economist and politician who was president of Brazil from 2011 to 2016, the first woman to hold the office. A former left-wing guerrilla imprisoned and tortured under the military dictatorship, she served as Lula's chief of staff before succeeding…

duong-tam-kha.s: Duong Tam Kha was a Vietnamese ruler who seized the throne of the Ngo dynasty after the death of his brother-in-law Ngo Quyen in 944, ruling as Duong Binh Vuong. Ngo Quyen's son Ngo Xuong Van overthrew him in 950 but spared his life.

dong-hoi.s: Dong Hoi is a coastal city in central Vietnam, capital of Quang Binh province. In the 17th century the Nguyen lords fortified the area with long defensive walls, the Dong Hoi and Truong Duc walls, which held off repeated Trinh offensives during the Trinh–Nguyen War of 1627 to…

dinuzulu-kacetshwayo.s: Dinuzulu kaCetshwayo was king of the Zulu from 1884 to 1913, the son of Cetshwayo. In 1884 he defeated his rival Zibhebhu with the help of Boer volunteers, who in return took much of western Zululand as the Nieuwe Republiek.

dharmakshema.s: Dharmakshema was an Indian Buddhist monk and translator who worked in China under the Northern Liang ruler Juqu Mengxun. At the Northern Liang capital Guzang, modern Wuwei, he translated many Mahayana scriptures into Chinese, above all the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, whose teaching…

dietrich-von-furstenberg.s: Dietrich von Fürstenberg was prince-bishop of Paderborn from 1585 to 1618. A leader of the Counter-Reformation in Westphalia, he suppressed Lutheranism in the city of Paderborn, which he brought to submission in 1604, and restored Catholicism across the prince-bishopric.

datong.s: Datong is a city in northern Shanxi province, China, near the Great Wall. As Pingcheng it was the capital of the Northern Wei dynasty from 398 until the move to Luoyang in 494, and the Yungang Grottoes were carved nearby.

dou-xian.s: Dou Xian was a Chinese general of the Eastern Han dynasty and brother of the regent Empress Dowager Dou. In 89 he led a Han army with Southern Xiongnu allies that routed the Northern Xiongnu, and the historian Ban Gu composed a victory inscription carved at Mount Yanran in…

durango-city.s: Durango, officially Victoria de Durango, is a city in north-western Mexico, capital of the state of Durango. It was founded in 1563 by Francisco de Ibarra as the capital of the province of Nueva Vizcaya, named after his native Biscay, and lies beside the Cerro de Mercado, a…

diyar-mudar.s: Diyar Mudar is the medieval Arabic name for the western part of the Jazira, the upper Mesopotamian region along the Euphrates and the Balikh, named after the Mudar tribes settled there in early Islamic times. Its main towns included Raqqa, Harran, Edessa and Saruj.

drasco.s: Drasco was a prince of the Obotrites, a West Slavic people of present-day Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein, and an ally of Charlemagne. In 798 he led the Obotrites to victory over the Nordalbingian Saxons near Bornhöved.

darzalas.s: Darzalas was a Thracian god worshipped as the Great God at the Greek colony of Odessos, modern Varna on the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria. Shown on the city's coins as a bearded figure holding a cornucopia and a dish, he was associated with fertility and the underworld.

dulo-clan.s: The Dulo clan was the ruling house of the early Bulgars, recorded in the Nominalia of the Bulgarian Khans. Its members included Kubrat, founder of Old Great Bulgaria in the 7th century, and his son Asparuh, who founded the First Bulgarian Empire.

dahshur.s: Dahshur is a royal necropolis on the west bank of the Nile south of Saqqara in Egypt. The Fourth Dynasty king Sneferu built two pyramids there in the 26th century BCE, the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid, the first true smooth-sided pyramid.

djoser.s: Djoser was a king of ancient Egypt's Third Dynasty who reigned in the 27th century BCE. His Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed according to tradition by his official Imhotep, was the first monumental stone building in Egypt.

david-moore-robinson.s: David Moore Robinson was an American classical archaeologist and professor at Johns Hopkins University. Between 1928 and 1938 he directed four seasons of excavation at Olynthus in northern Greece, uncovering whole districts of Classical houses with mosaics and household goods.

doris-greece.s: Doris is a small mountainous region of central Greece, in the upper valley of the Cephissus between Mount Oeta and Mount Parnassus. The ancient Greeks regarded it as the homeland of the Dorians, and Sparta honoured it as its mother country.

darul-islam-indonesia.s: Darul Islam was an Islamist rebel movement that fought to establish an Islamic State of Indonesia. Its leader Sekarmadji Maridjan Kartosuwiryo proclaimed the state in West Java in 1949, and revolts in South Sulawesi, South Kalimantan and Aceh, where Daud Beureueh rose in 1953,…

demetrius-ii-aetolicus.s: Demetrius II Aetolicus was king of Macedon from 239 to 229 BCE, the son of Antigonus II Gonatas. Most of his reign was spent in the Demetrian War against the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues, which allied against him.

diaeus.s: Diaeus was a general of the Achaean League who, with Critolaus, led it into its final war against Rome. Taking command after Critolaus' defeat in 146 BCE, he freed and armed slaves and raised a last army, which Lucius Mummius destroyed on the Isthmus near Corinth.

domitius-alexander.s: Domitius Alexander was a Roman usurper who proclaimed himself emperor in Africa around 308, rebelling against Maxentius, who ruled Italy. As vicar of the diocese of Africa he controlled Carthage and the grain supply to Rome for about three years.

deodhai.s: The Deodhais were one of the hereditary priestly groups of the Ahom people of Assam, alongside the Bailungs and the Mohans. They preserved the older Tai rites, language and script of the founders of the Ahom kingdom, conducted royal and ancestral ceremonies and were custodians…

dikhow-river.s: The Dikhow is a river of Upper Assam in north-east India, a south-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra. It rises in the hills of Nagaland and flows north-west through the town of Sivasagar to join the Brahmaputra.

dimasa-kingdom.s: The Dimasa Kingdom, often called the Kachari kingdom, was a state of the Dimasa people in present-day Assam and Nagaland, India. Its capital was at Dimapur until the Ahom king Suhungmung sacked the city in 1536, after which the court moved to Maibong and later to Khaspur in…

duchy-of-alamannia.s: The Duchy of Alamannia was a territory of the Frankish kingdom covering the lands of the Alemanni, roughly present-day south-west Germany, Alsace and north-eastern Switzerland. Formed after the Merovingians absorbed the Alemanni in the early sixth century, it was ruled by…

dardanians.s: The Dardanians were an ancient people of the central Balkans, living in the region of present-day Kosovo, southern Serbia and north-western North Macedonia. Warlike northern neighbours of Macedon, they raided it repeatedly in the Hellenistic period, and King Demetrius II died…

drago-doctrine.s: The Drago Doctrine was the principle, announced in 1902 by the Argentine foreign minister Luis María Drago, that no foreign power may use armed force to collect public debts from an American state. It was a response to the naval blockade of Venezuela by Britain, Germany and…

dionysia.s: The Dionysia were Athenian festivals of the god Dionysus, the greatest being the City Dionysia held each spring. From the late sixth century BCE it included contests in tragedy, later also comedy and satyr plays, for which the works of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and…

decelea.s: Decelea was a deme of northern Attica on the route from Athens to Euboea and Boeotia. In 413 BCE, on the advice of the exiled Alcibiades, Sparta occupied and fortified it as a permanent base, cutting Athens off from its farmland and the Laurium silver mines and causing…

dharmashastra.s: Dharmashastra is the body of Sanskrit treatises on dharma, the religious and legal duties of Hindus, of which the Laws of Manu is the best known. They cover the duties of kings and castes, family law, inheritance and penance.

dae-ijin.s: Dae Ijin was the eleventh king of Balhae, reigning from 830 to 857, and grandson of King Seon, under whom the kingdom had reached its greatest extent. His long reign was peaceful and stable, with regular embassies to Tang China and to Japan, and he continued the adoption of…

dae-inseon.s: Dae Inseon was the fifteenth and last king of Balhae, reigning from about 906 to 926. When the Khitan under Yelü Abaoji invaded at the end of 925, they took the western fortress of Buyeo and besieged the capital Sanggyeong, and Dae Inseon surrendered early in 926.

dae-jung-sang.s: Dae Jung-sang was a leader of Goguryeo refugees in the Yingzhou region of Tang China and the father of Dae Joyeong, founder of Balhae. When the Khitan rose against the Tang in 696, he and the Mohe chief Geolsa Biu led their followers east towards Manchuria.

dae-munye.s: Dae Munye was a prince of Balhae, younger brother of King Mu, who had lived as a hostage at the Tang court. When Mu ordered an attack on the Heishui Mohe in the 720s because they had placed themselves under Tang protection, Dae Munye opposed the war and fled to Tang China.

dengzhou.s: Dengzhou was a prefecture and port on the northern coast of the Shandong peninsula in China, at modern Penglai, facing the Bohai Strait. It was a main harbour for sea traffic between China, Korea and Manchuria.

dunhua.s: Dunhua is a city in Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture in Jilin province, north-east China, on the upper Mudan River. Near it, around Mount Dongmo, Dae Joyeong founded the state that became Balhae in 698, and the city is identified with the first Balhae capital.

dakhil-darwaza.s: The Dakhil Darwaza is the monumental brick gateway of the citadel of Gaur, in Malda district, West Bengal, India. Usually dated to the reign of Rukunuddin Barbak Shah in the fifteenth century, it rises about 21 metres, with tapering corner towers and fine terracotta ornament,…

decelean-war.s: The Decelean War, also called the Ionian War, was the final phase of the Peloponnesian War, from 413 to 404 BCE. On the advice of Alcibiades, Sparta fortified Decelea in Attica as a permanent base, cutting Athens off from its countryside and silver mines, while the war shifted…

dynamis-bosporan-queen.s: Dynamis was queen of the Bosporan Kingdom in the late first century BCE, a daughter of Pharnaces II and granddaughter of Mithridates VI of Pontus. She married Asander and, after his death around 17 BCE, briefly the usurper Scribonius and then Polemon I of Pontus, whom Rome…

dadabhai-naoroji.s: Dadabhai Naoroji was an Indian political leader, economist and scholar from a Parsi family of Bombay. In Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) he developed the 'drain theory', arguing that British rule drained India's wealth through home charges and profits.

delhi-durbar.s: The Delhi Durbars were imperial assemblies held at Delhi to mark the accession of British monarchs as rulers of India. The first, in 1877, proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India; the second, in 1903, celebrated Edward VII; and the third, in 1911, was attended in person by…

delian-league.s: The Delian League was an alliance of Greek city-states founded in 478 BCE under Athenian leadership to continue the war against Persia, with its treasury first on the island of Delos. Members contributed ships or money, and Athens gradually turned the league into an empire,…

david-baird.s: Sir David Baird was a Scottish general in the British Army. After years as a prisoner of Hyder Ali in India, he led the storming of Seringapatam in 1799.

diodorus-siculus.s: Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian from Agyrium in Sicily who wrote the Bibliotheca historica, a universal history in forty books from mythical times to about 60 BCE. Fifteen books survive complete and others in fragments.

damme.s: Damme is a small town in West Flanders, Belgium, north-east of Bruges. Founded in the late twelfth century on the Zwin inlet, it served as the outport of Bruges, where goods passed between sea-going ships and the city.

douai.s: Douai is a town on the river Scarpe in the Nord department of northern France. In the Middle Ages it was one of the great cloth towns of the County of Flanders; it passed to the French crown in 1312, returned to Flanders in 1369 and became French for good when Louis XIV took…

dunkirk.s: Dunkirk is a port city on the North Sea in the Nord department of France, close to the Belgian border. Part of the County of Flanders in the Middle Ages, it changed hands repeatedly between Spain, France and England until Louis XIV bought it from Charles II of England in 1662.

dit-of-peronne.s: The Dit of Péronne was the arbitration award given by King Louis IX of France at Péronne in September 1256 to end the War of the Flemish Succession. It settled the feud between the children of Countess Margaret II of Flanders and Hainaut: her Dampierre sons were to inherit…

drassanes-reials-de-barcelona.s: The Drassanes Reials are the medieval royal shipyards of Barcelona, begun in the late thirteenth century under Peter III of Aragon and enlarged in the fourteenth. Their great vaulted halls built the galleys of the Crown of Aragon's Mediterranean fleets.

dukla-pass.s: The Dukla Pass is a low pass in the Carpathian Mountains on the border between Poland and Slovakia. In September to November 1944 Soviet and Czechoslovak forces fought a costly battle there in an attempt to reach the Slovak National Uprising.

dissolution-of-czechoslovakia.s: The dissolution of Czechoslovakia, known as the Velvet Divorce, divided the federation into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993. After the June 1992 elections, the Czech and Slovak leaders Václav Klaus and Vladimír Mečiar agreed on separation, which the Federal…

dunchad-becc.s: Dúnchad Becc was king of Kintyre, of the Cenél nGabráin, in the early eighth century, and died in 721. In 719 he defeated Selbach of the rival Cenél Loairn in a sea battle off Ardde Anesbi, the earliest naval battle recorded in the British Isles, in the long rivalry for the…

dar-fertit.s: Dar Fertit, the land of the Fertit, was the name given in Darfur to the country south of the sultanate, in what is now western South Sudan and the north-east of the Central African Republic. Its varied peoples, called Fertit, were raided for slaves by the sultans of Darfur and…

daulat-khan-lodi.s: Daulat Khan Lodi was the governor of the Punjab under the Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi. Fearing the sultan, he invited the Timurid ruler Babur of Kabul to invade India in the early 1520s, but then turned against him.

delphic-amphictyony.s: The Delphic Amphictyony was a religious league of twelve peoples of central and northern Greece that met at Anthela near Thermopylae and at Delphi. It protected the sanctuary of Apollo, ran the Pythian Games and declared the Sacred Wars against those accused of violating the…

danish-asiatic-company.s: The Danish Asiatic Company was a trading company chartered in Copenhagen in 1732 with a monopoly of Danish trade with Asia. Its ships sailed to Canton for tea, silk and porcelain and to the Danish colony of Tranquebar in India, and it was among the most profitable enterprises…

dilmun-burial-mounds.s: The Dilmun Burial Mounds are the tens of thousands of earth and stone tumuli built across northern Bahrain mainly between about 2050 and 1750 BCE, in the Early Dilmun period. They range from small individual graves to large royal tombs at A'ali.

dieric-bouts.s: Dieric Bouts was an Early Netherlandish painter, born in Haarlem around 1415, who worked in Leuven from the 1440s and became its official city painter in 1468. His best-known work is the Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament in St Peter's Church, Leuven, with its Last Supper, and…

declaration-of-meudon.s: The Declaration of Meudon was a secret agreement of 30 September 1736 by which Stanisław Leszczyński, the deposed king of Poland who was to receive the duchies of Lorraine and Bar for life, handed their administration and revenues to an intendant named by his son-in-law Louis…

dieuze.s: Dieuze is a small town in the Moselle department of north-eastern France, on the Seille. Its salt springs were worked from the Middle Ages, and the saltworks of Dieuze were a major source of income first for the dukes of Lorraine and later for the French crown.

domremy-la-pucelle.s: Domrémy-la-Pucelle is a village on the Meuse in the Vosges department of north-eastern France. It is the birthplace of Joan of Arc, born there around 1412, and her family house survives as a museum.

donato-bramante.s: Donato Bramante was an Italian architect and painter, born near Urbino, who worked at the Sforza court in Milan from the late 1470s until 1499, building the church of Santa Maria presso San Satiro and the domed tribune of Santa Maria delle Grazie. In Rome he became the leading…

dives-sur-mer.s: Dives-sur-Mer is a small town in the Calvados department of Normandy, at the mouth of the Dives. In the summer of 1066 Duke William of Normandy assembled his invasion fleet there before moving it to Saint-Valery-sur-Somme and crossing to England.

dudo-of-saint-quentin.s: Dudo of Saint-Quentin was a canon from the Vermandois who came to the Norman court as an envoy and, at the request of Richard I and Richard II, wrote a history of the first rulers of Normandy, De moribus et actis primorum Normanniae ducum. Completed around 1015, it gives a…

diponegoro.s: Diponegoro was a Javanese prince of the Yogyakarta sultanate who led the Java War against Dutch rule from 1825 to 1830. The eldest son of Sultan Hamengkubuwono III, he drew support from peasants, Muslim scholars and nobles angered by colonial interference and taxation.

dutch-indonesian-round-table-conference.s: The Dutch–Indonesian Round Table Conference met in The Hague from August to November 1949, bringing together the Netherlands, the Republic of Indonesia and the federal states created by the Dutch. It agreed that the Netherlands would transfer sovereignty to the Republic of the…

dutch-golden-age.s: The Dutch Golden Age was the period, roughly the seventeenth century, when the Dutch Republic was among the richest and most powerful states in Europe. Amsterdam dominated world trade and finance, the East and West India Companies built an overseas empire, and the Republic led…

dutch-water-line.s: The Dutch Water Line was a defensive line of fortified towns and low land that could be deliberately flooded, protecting the heartland of Holland on its eastern side. First used on a large scale in 1672, when it halted the armies of Louis XIV short of Amsterdam, it was later…

dawachi.s: Dawachi was the last khan of the Dzungar Khanate, a grandson of the general Tsering Dondub. In 1753, with the help of the Khoid prince Amursana, he killed Lama Dorji and seized power, but the two soon fell out and Amursana went over to the Qing.

division-of-leipzig.s: The Division of Leipzig of 1485 split the lands of the house of Wettin between the brothers Ernest and Albert. Ernest kept the electoral title with Wittenberg and most of Thuringia, founding the Ernestine line, while Albert received Meissen with Dresden and Leipzig, founding…

dresden-frauenkirche.s: The Frauenkirche in Dresden is a Lutheran church built between 1726 and 1743 to designs by George Bähr and crowned by a great stone dome, a landmark of Baroque Dresden. Destroyed in the Allied bombing of February 1945, it remained a ruin and war memorial throughout the East…

dionysiou-monastery.s: Dionysiou Monastery is an Eastern Orthodox monastery on Mount Athos in Greece, built on a rock above the sea on the peninsula's south-west coast. It was founded in the 1370s by the monk Dionysios of Korisos with the support of Emperor Alexios III of Trebizond, whose chrysobull…

deutz.s: Deutz is a district of Cologne on the right bank of the Rhine, opposite the old city. It began as Divitia, a fort built by Constantine the Great around 310 together with a permanent bridge over the Rhine, to secure Cologne against the Franks.

der-spiegel.s: Der Spiegel is a German weekly news magazine founded in Hanover in 1947 and published in Hamburg since 1952, led for decades by Rudolf Augstein. Known for investigative journalism, it was at the centre of the Spiegel affair of 1962, when its offices were searched and editors…

die-zeit.s: Die Zeit is a German weekly newspaper founded in Hamburg in 1946. Known for long political and cultural articles, it was shaped by journalists such as Marion Gräfin Dönhoff, and from 1983 the former chancellor Helmut Schmidt served as one of its publishers.

dahra.s: The Dahra is a coastal mountain range in north-western Algeria, between the Chelif valley and the Mediterranean. In June 1845 French troops under Aimable Pélissier lit fires at the mouths of caves where members of the Ouled Riah tribe had taken refuge, killing hundreds of men,…

dinder-river.s: The Dinder River is a seasonal tributary of the Blue Nile that rises in the Ethiopian highlands west of Lake Tana and joins the Blue Nile in eastern Sudan below Sennar. In 1744 Funj forces defeated an invading army of the Ethiopian emperor Iyasu II on its banks.

damjing.s: Damjing was a Buddhist monk from Goguryeo who went to Japan in 610 together with another monk. According to the Nihon shoki, he was learned in the Confucian classics and introduced the making of paper, ink and pigments, as well as millstones.

dongcheon-of-goguryeo.s: Dongcheon was the eleventh king of Goguryeo, reigning from 227 to 248. He allied with the Chinese state of Cao Wei against the Gongsun warlords of Liaodong but then attacked Wei territory in 242.

dongmaeng.s: Dongmaeng was a great state festival of Goguryeo held in the tenth month of the year to give thanks to Heaven, recorded in the Chinese Records of the Three Kingdoms. The whole country assembled for sacrifices, singing and dancing.

duden.s: Duden was a Mongol prince of the Golden Horde, sent by Khan Tokhta to intervene in the quarrels of the Russian princes. In 1293 his army sacked Vladimir, Moscow, Suzdal and more than a dozen other towns of north-eastern Rus' in support of Prince Andrey of Gorodets.

dobyeongmasa.s: The Dobyeongmasa was a joint council of senior ministers of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo, first set up to deliberate on frontier defence. Renamed the Dopyeong-uisasa in 1279 and widened in membership, it became the real centre of government in the late Goryeo period.

dantons-death.s: Danton's Death is a play by Georg Büchner, written in 1835 while he was hiding from the Hessian police after publishing a revolutionary pamphlet. It portrays the last days of the French revolutionary Georges Danton before his execution under Robespierre's Terror, using…

der-hessische-landbote.s: Der Hessische Landbote was a revolutionary pamphlet written by Georg Büchner and edited by Friedrich Ludwig Weidig, secretly printed and distributed in the Grand Duchy of Hesse in 1834. Under the motto Peace to the huts!

duchy-of-westphalia.s: The Duchy of Westphalia was a territory in north-western Germany, centred on the Sauerland and Arnsberg. After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180 it was granted to the archbishops of Cologne, who ruled it until 1803.

departement-des-forets.s: The Département des Forêts was a department of the French Republic and Empire from 1795 to 1814, formed from most of the former Duchy of Luxembourg after its annexation by revolutionary France. Its capital was the city of Luxembourg, and it was named after the forests of the…

dormition-cathedral-moscow.s: The Dormition Cathedral is the principal church of the Moscow Kremlin, rebuilt in 1475–1479 by the Italian architect Aristotele Fioravanti for Ivan III on the model of the cathedral at Vladimir. It served as the mother church of Muscovy and later of the Russian Orthodox…

dhruva-dharavarsha.s: Dhruva Dharavarsha was a king of the Rashtrakuta dynasty of the Deccan who reigned from about 780 to 793. Seizing the throne from his elder brother, he led the first Rashtrakuta expedition to the north around 786, defeating the Pratihara Vatsaraja and the Pala Dharmapala in…

don-quixote.s: Don Quixote is a novel by Miguel de Cervantes, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615. It tells of a Spanish gentleman who, his mind turned by reading chivalric romances, sets out as a knight-errant with his squire Sancho Panza.

daura.s: Daura is a town in Katsina State in northern Nigeria, regarded in Hausa tradition as the oldest of the Hausa states. According to the legend of Bayajidda, a prince from the east killed a sacred snake in the town's well and married its queen, and their descendants founded the…

dvaita-vedanta.s: Dvaita Vedanta is a dualist school of Hindu philosophy founded by Madhvacharya in the 13th century in coastal Karnataka. It teaches that God, identified with Vishnu, individual souls and matter are eternally distinct, in contrast to the non-dualism of Advaita.

dairatul-maarifil-osmania.s: The Dairatul Maarifil Osmania is a learned society and press in Hyderabad, founded in 1888 under the patronage of the Nizam, that edits and publishes classical Arabic manuscripts. Its editions of works of history, hadith, medicine, astronomy and mathematics made many texts…

djuanda-declaration.s: The Djuanda Declaration was issued on 13 December 1957 by the Indonesian prime minister Djuanda Kartawidjaja. It declared that all waters around, between and connecting the islands of Indonesia formed part of the national territory, replacing the narrow colonial-era…

deskaheh.s: Deskaheh, born Levi General, was a Cayuga chief and speaker of the traditional council of the Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario. In 1923 he travelled to Geneva on a Haudenosaunee passport to ask the League of Nations to recognise the Six Nations as a sovereign people.

dong-jieyuan.s: Dong Jieyuan was a writer of the Jin dynasty, active in the late twelfth century, whose real name is unknown; Jieyuan was an honorific title for a top examination candidate. He wrote a long version of the Romance of the Western Chamber in the zhugongdiao form, a sung narrative…

donghak.s: Donghak ('Eastern Learning') is a Korean religious movement founded in 1860 by Choe Je-u. It combined Confucian, Buddhist, Daoist and shamanist ideas with worship of a supreme god, and it presented itself as a native alternative to Catholicism.

duguwa-dynasty.s: The Duguwa were the first ruling dynasty of the Kingdom of Kanem, north-east of Lake Chad. Known from the royal chronicle of Kanem and from Arab geographers, who linked the kingdom with the Zaghawa people, they ruled from around the ninth century until the late eleventh century.

diwan-lughat-al-turk.s: The Diwan Lughat al-Turk ('Compendium of the Languages of the Turks') is a dictionary of the Turkic languages written in Arabic by Mahmud al-Kashgari, a member of the Kara-Khanid dynasty, in Baghdad in the 1070s. Besides words, it records Turkic poetry, proverbs, tribes and…

dasht-i-qipchaq.s: The Dasht-i Qipchaq, "the Kipchak steppe", was the Persian name for the great grassland stretching from the Black Sea across the Volga and Ural rivers to the Irtysh and the Syr Darya. It took its name from the Kipchak nomads who dominated it from the eleventh century.

daroca.s: Daroca is a historic town in the province of Zaragoza in Aragon, on the Jiloca river. A Muslim fortress town, it was taken by Alfonso I of Aragon around 1120 and became an important frontier stronghold, with its own charter of 1142 and a long circuit of walls and towers that…

der-blaue-reiter.s: Der Blaue Reiter, "the Blue Rider", was a group of artists formed in Munich in 1911 by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, joined by painters such as August Macke, Gabriele Münter and Paul Klee. Its exhibitions and its almanac of 1912 promoted expressive colour and abstraction…

daudi-chwa-ii.s: Daudi Chwa II was kabaka of Buganda from 1897 until his death in 1939. He was installed as an infant after his father Mwanga II rebelled against the British, and regents led by Apolo Kagwa governed until he came of age in 1914.

duhaga-ii-of-bunyoro.s: Andereya Duhaga II was omukama of Bunyoro from 1902 to 1924, installed by the British after the deposition of his brother Kitahimbwa. He ruled a kingdom treated as conquered territory, with Ganda chiefs placed over Nyoro districts, which provoked the Nyangire revolt of 1907.

dominicus-gundissalinus.s: Dominicus Gundissalinus was a Castilian philosopher and translator, archdeacon of Cuéllar, who worked in Toledo. With collaborators such as Abraham ibn Daud he translated Arabic philosophical works into Latin, among them parts of Avicenna's "Book of the Healing", al-Farabi and…

dahomey-amazons.s: The Dahomey Amazons were the corps of women soldiers of the Kingdom of Dahomey, known locally as ahosi, "king's wives", or mino, "our mothers". Formed from palace guards in the eighteenth century and much expanded under Ghezo, they numbered several thousand at their height.

dakodonou.s: Dakodonou is remembered in the traditions of Dahomey as an early ruler of the Fon on the Abomey plateau, who reigned in the first half of the seventeenth century before Houegbadja. Tradition credits him with seizing land from local chiefs, laying the foundations of the…

do-aklin.s: Do-Aklin is remembered in the traditions of Dahomey as the leader of the royal family that migrated from Allada to the Abomey plateau around 1600, after a succession dispute in the Kingdom of Allada. He is regarded as the ancestor and first chief of the line that later founded…

danish-code.s: The Danish Code was the law code issued by Christian V of Denmark in 1683, replacing the medieval provincial laws with a single code for the whole kingdom. It reflected the absolute monarchy created in 1660, and a parallel Norwegian Code followed in 1687.

danegeld.s: Danegeld was a tax raised in Anglo-Saxon England to pay tribute to Viking raiders, above all from 991 under Æthelred the Unready, when large sums were paid to Danish armies to stop their attacks. Later the name was used for a land tax collected by English kings, including…

declaration-of-the-rights-of-man-and-of-.n: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
declaration-of-the-rights-of-man-and-of-.s: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted by the French National Constituent Assembly on 26 August 1789. Drawing on Enlightenment ideas, it declared that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, that sovereignty lies with the nation, and that…

denis-diderot.s: Denis Diderot was a French philosopher and writer, a leading figure of the Enlightenment. For over twenty years he edited the Encyclopédie, overcoming bans and censorship to complete it.

david-komnenos.s: David Komnenos was a grandson of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos I who, with his brother Alexios, seized Trebizond in April 1204 with Georgian troops provided by their kinswoman Queen Tamar. While Alexios ruled as the first emperor of Trebizond, David led campaigns westward…

daniel-defoe.s: Daniel Defoe was an English writer, journalist and merchant. A Dissenter and pamphleteer, he was pilloried for satire in 1703 and later worked as a government agent in Scotland during the negotiations for the Union of 1707.

david-hume.s: David Hume was a Scottish philosopher, historian and essayist, one of the leading figures of the Scottish Enlightenment. His Treatise of Human Nature and later Enquiries argued that knowledge rests on experience and habit, raising radical sceptical questions about causation…

dolforwyn-castle.s: Dolforwyn Castle is a ruined Welsh castle in Powys, mid Wales, built by Llywelyn ap Gruffudd from 1273 above the Severn valley near Montgomery. Edward I forbade its construction, and the dispute added to the tensions that led to war in 1277, when English forces besieged and…

david-vii-ulu.s: David VII, called Ulu ('the Elder'), was king of Georgia from 1247 to 1270, reigning at first jointly with his cousin David VI Narin under Mongol overlordship. An illegitimate son of George IV, he was recognised by the Mongols as co-king, and after David Narin withdrew to…

dependency-of-ireland-on-great-britain-a.n: Dependency of Ireland on Great Britain Act 1719
dependency-of-ireland-on-great-britain-a.s: The Dependency of Ireland on Great Britain Act, known as the Declaratory Act, was passed by the British Parliament in 1720. It declared that the Parliament at Westminster had full power to make laws binding Ireland and removed the appellate jurisdiction of the Irish House of…

derry.s: Derry, officially Londonderry, is a city on the River Foyle in the north-west of Northern Ireland. It grew from a sixth-century monastery associated with Saint Columba and was rebuilt by the City of London companies during the Plantation of Ulster, its walls being completed in…

drogheda.s: Drogheda is a port town on the River Boyne in County Louth, eastern Ireland. Founded by the Anglo-Normans, it was one of the principal walled towns of the English colony and sometimes hosted the Irish Parliament, including the one that passed Poynings' Law in 1494.

deuteronomistic-history.s: The Deuteronomistic History is the name scholars give to the books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, read as a single historical work shaped by the language and theology of Deuteronomy. Proposed by Martin Noth in 1943, the theory holds that it was compiled in Judah in the…

daria-daulat-bagh.s: Daria Daulat Bagh is the summer palace of Tipu Sultan at Srirangapatna in Karnataka, India, built in 1784 in the Indo-Islamic style and set in a large garden. Its teak walls are covered with painted murals, among them a large scene of the victory of Hyder Ali and Tipu over the…

dogana-della-mena-delle-pecore-di-puglia.n: Dogana della mena delle pecore di Puglia
dogana-della-mena-delle-pecore-di-puglia.s: The Dogana della mena delle pecore di Puglia was the royal customs office founded by Alfonso V of Aragon in 1447 to regulate the seasonal migration of sheep between the Abruzzi mountains and the plain of Apulia. Based at Foggia, it allocated winter pastures on the Tavoliere…

dipendra-of-nepal.s: Dipendra (1971–2001) was the crown prince of Nepal, the eldest son of King Birendra. On 1 June 2001, at a family gathering in Narayanhiti Palace, he shot dead his father, his mother Queen Aishwarya and other members of the royal family, according to the official inquiry,…

david-ochterlony.s: Sir David Ochterlony (1758–1825) was a Boston-born general of the British East India Company. In the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–1816 he was the most successful British commander, forcing Amar Singh Thapa to surrender in 1815 and advancing towards Kathmandu in 1816, which led…

divya-upadesh.s: The Divya Upadesh ("Divine Counsel") is the set of final political teachings of Prithvi Narayan Shah, the founder of unified Nepal, delivered to his courtiers at Nuwakot shortly before his death in 1775 and recorded by them. It describes Nepal as "a yam between two boulders",…

dore-south-yorkshire.s: Dore is a former village, now a suburb of Sheffield, which lay on the medieval boundary between Mercia and Northumbria; its name means a pass or door. According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, in 829 Ecgberht of Wessex, having conquered Mercia, led his army to Dore, where the…

denis-of-portugal.s: Denis (Dinis) was king of Portugal from 1279 to 1325. He fixed the border with Castile by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, founded the university in Lisbon in 1290, made Portuguese the language of government and founded the Order of Christ in 1319 to take over the Templars'…

dominique-mbonyumutwa.s: Dominique Mbonyumutwa was a Rwandan Hutu politician and sub-chief. On 1 November 1959 he was attacked by young Tutsi activists, and false rumours of his death set off the violence against Tutsi chiefs that began the Rwandan Revolution.

david-ii-of-scotland.s: David II was King of Scots from 1329 to 1371, the son of Robert the Bruce. Driven into exile in France by Edward Balliol and the English in 1334, he returned in 1341, but in 1346 he invaded England, was defeated and captured at Neville's Cross and was held in England for…

david-ii-of-imereti.s: David II was King of Imereti in western Georgia from 1784 to 1789. He succeeded Solomon I but struggled against rival claimants and powerful nobles, and in 1789 he was overthrown by Solomon II, a grandson of Erekle II of Kartli-Kakheti, who had eastern Georgian support.

declaration-of-arbroath.s: The Declaration of Arbroath is a letter dated 6 April 1320 from the barons and community of Scotland to Pope John XXII, asking him to recognise Robert I as king and Scotland as independent of England. It famously declares that the Scots would remove even Robert if he submitted…

donald-ii-of-scotland.s: Donald II, in Gaelic Domnall mac Causantín, was king of the Picts or of Alba from 889 to 900. He was the first ruler whose death notice in the Irish annals calls him king of Alba, the name that replaced Pictland for the kingdom north of the Forth.

dag-hammarskjold.s: Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish economist and diplomat who served as Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1953 to 1961. He expanded the role of the office, developing UN peacekeeping during the Suez Crisis of 1956.

dicalydones.s: The Dicalydones were one of the two peoples into which the Picts were divided according to the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, writing of the 360s, the other being the Verturiones. Their name appears to be linked to the earlier Caledonians, and they probably lived in…

dundurn.s: Dundurn is a hill fort near St Fillans at the eastern end of Loch Earn in Perthshire, Scotland. Excavations have shown that its summit was fortified in the early Middle Ages, and it is usually identified with the Dún Duirn recorded as besieged in 683 in the Irish annals.

dunnottar-castle.s: Dunnottar Castle is a ruined fortress on a rocky headland on the north-east coast of Scotland, south of Stonehaven in Aberdeenshire. The site is identified with Dún Foither, a Pictish stronghold recorded in the Irish annals as besieged in 681 and 694, and Vikings attacked it…

dupplin-cross.s: The Dupplin Cross is a carved stone cross of about 800 that once stood on a hillside near Forteviot in Perthshire, Scotland. Its Latin inscription names Custantin son of Fergus, the Pictish king Constantín who ruled from 789 to 820.

dal-riata.s: Dál Riata was a Gaelic kingdom that spanned the western seaboard of Scotland, centred on Argyll, and part of County Antrim in Ireland, from about the sixth to the ninth century. Its kings ruled from strongholds such as Dunadd, and the monastery of Iona, founded by Columba…

dorchester-on-thames.s: Dorchester-on-Thames is a village in Oxfordshire on the River Thame near its confluence with the Thames. A Roman small town, it lay at the heart of early West Saxon settlement, and in 635 Bishop Birinus baptised King Cynegils there and made it the seat of the first West Saxon…

david-friedrich-strauss.s: David Friedrich Strauss was a German theologian and writer from Ludwigsburg, a pupil of Ferdinand Christian Baur at Tübingen. His Life of Jesus (1835–1836) treated the gospel miracles as myths shaped by early Christian belief, caused a sensation and cost him his academic career.

dragisa-cvetkovic.s: Dragiša Cvetković was a Serbian politician who served as prime minister of Yugoslavia from 1939 to 1941. He concluded the 1939 agreement with Vladko Maček that created the Banovina of Croatia, and under heavy German pressure his government signed the Tripartite Pact in Vienna…

dusan-simovic.s: Dušan Simović was a Yugoslav general and commander of the air force who led the coup of 27 March 1941 that overthrew the regency of Prince Paul after Yugoslavia joined the Tripartite Pact. Declaring the young Peter II of age, he became prime minister, but Germany invaded on 6…

daedalus.s: Daedalus is a craftsman and inventor of Greek mythology, said to have built the Labyrinth at Knossos for King Minos to hold the Minotaur. Imprisoned by Minos, he escaped on wings of feathers and wax that he made for himself and his son Icarus, who flew too near the sun and…

dreros.s: Dreros is an ancient Greek city in eastern Crete, near modern Neapoli. It preserves a law inscribed around 650–600 BCE limiting repeated tenure of the office of kosmos, one of the earliest surviving Greek laws on stone, and an early temple of Apollo Delphinios with hammered…

dai-viet-su-ky-toan-thu.n: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư
dai-viet-su-ky-toan-thu.s: The Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, the "Complete Annals of Đại Việt", is the official national chronicle of Vietnam, written in classical Chinese. Compiled by Ngô Sĩ Liên and completed in 1479 under Lê Thánh Tông, it was extended by later historians and printed in 1697.

dule-temple.s: Dule Temple is a Buddhist temple in Ji County, Tianjin, China. Its Guanyin Pavilion, rebuilt in 984 under the Liao dynasty, is one of the oldest surviving wooden buildings in China, a two-storey hall built around a 16-metre clay statue of the bodhisattva Guanyin.

diocese-of-hispania.s: The Diocese of Hispania, or Diocese of the Spains, was a civil administrative unit of the late Roman Empire created by Diocletian's reforms around 300. It grouped the provinces of the Iberian Peninsula, among them Lusitania, Baetica, Carthaginiensis, Tarraconensis and…

dewan-rakyat.s: The Dewan Rakyat ('House of the People') is the lower house of the Parliament of Malaysia, with 222 members elected for up to five years from single-member constituencies. The prime minister must command its confidence, and it passes legislation and the budget, while the…

djinguereber-mosque.s: The Djinguereber Mosque is the great mosque of Timbuktu in Mali, a landmark of earthen Sudano-Sahelian architecture. Tradition credits its building to Mansa Musa after his return from pilgrimage in the 1320s, to designs by the Andalusi poet-architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, and…

dispositio-achillea.s: The Dispositio Achillea was the house law issued in 1473 by Albert Achilles, Elector of Brandenburg, to regulate the Hohenzollern succession. It laid down that the Mark of Brandenburg with the electoral dignity should pass undivided to the eldest son, while the Franconian…

david-alfaro-siqueiros.s: David Alfaro Siqueiros was a Mexican painter, one of the three great artists of the Mexican mural movement with Diego Rivera and José Clemente Orozco. A committed communist, he experimented with industrial paints and techniques and painted large political murals in Mexico, the…

diego-rivera.s: Diego Rivera was a Mexican painter and a leading figure of the Mexican mural movement. From the 1920s he painted large frescoes of Mexican history, Indigenous life and industrial labour in public buildings, including the National Palace in Mexico City and the Detroit Industry…

deir-el-bersha.s: Deir el-Bersha is an ancient cemetery on the east bank of the Nile in Middle Egypt, opposite Mallawi. Its rock-cut tombs belonged mainly to the nomarchs of the Hare nome in the Middle Kingdom.

dialogue-of-a-man-and-his-ba.n: Dialogue of a Man and His Ba
dialogue-of-a-man-and-his-ba.s: The Dialogue of a Man and His Ba is an Egyptian literary text of the Middle Kingdom, preserved on a single papyrus now in Berlin. In it a man weary of life argues with his ba, his soul, about death and suicide, in a mixture of prose and poems.

djehutyhotep.s: Djehutyhotep was a nomarch of the Hare nome in Middle Egypt under the Twelfth Dynasty kings Amenemhat II, Senusret II and Senusret III. His rock-cut tomb at Deir el-Bersha contains a celebrated painting of a colossal alabaster statue of him being hauled on a sledge by teams of…

didyma.s: Didyma was a sanctuary of Apollo on the west coast of Asia Minor, about 16 kilometres south of Miletus, which controlled it and was linked to it by a Sacred Way. Its oracle, run in archaic times by the Branchidae family, was sacked by the Persians after the Ionian Revolt.

donglin-movement.s: The Donglin movement was a group of Confucian scholar-officials of the late Ming dynasty centred on the Donglin Academy at Wuxi, revived by Gu Xiancheng in 1604. Its members called for moral renewal and attacked corruption and eunuch power at court, and their factional…

duarte-barbosa.s: Duarte Barbosa was a Portuguese writer and official who served in India as a scribe and interpreter from around 1500. His Book of Duarte Barbosa, completed about 1516, is one of the earliest European accounts of the Indian Ocean world, describing the towns of the East African…

dachau-concentration-camp.s: Dachau concentration camp, near Munich, was the first regular Nazi concentration camp, opened in March 1933 for political prisoners. It became the model for the SS camp system and later held Jews, Roma, clergy, Soviet prisoners of war and others from across Europe; more than…

deerfield-massachusetts.s: Deerfield is a town in the Connecticut River valley of western Massachusetts, settled by English colonists in the 1670s. It was a frontier outpost in the wars with New France, and on 29 February 1704 a French and Native raiding party destroyed much of the village, killing 56…

dolores-hidalgo.s: Dolores Hidalgo is a town in the Mexican state of Guanajuato. On 16 September 1810 its parish priest, Miguel Hidalgo, rang the church bell and called his parishioners to revolt, the Cry of Dolores that began the Mexican War of Independence.

david-lange.s: David Lange was Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1984 to 1989, leading the Fourth Labour Government. His government banned nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered ships, causing a rift with the United States in the ANZUS alliance, while his finance minister Roger Douglas carried…

dong-khanh.s: Đồng Khánh was emperor of Vietnam of the Nguyen dynasty from 1885 to 1889. After the regent Tôn Thất Thuyết fled from Huế with the young emperor Hàm Nghi to lead the Cần Vương resistance, the French placed Hàm Nghi's elder brother on the throne.

decembrists.s: The Decembrists were Russian army officers and nobles who staged a revolt in St Petersburg on 14 December 1825 (Old Style), refusing to swear allegiance to Nicholas I and seeking a constitution or a republic and the end of serfdom. The rising, and a second in the south, was…

descent-of-the-ganges.s: The Descent of the Ganges, also called Arjuna's Penance, is a huge open-air relief carved on two adjoining granite boulders at Mamallapuram in Tamil Nadu in the Pallava period, probably in the seventh century. Its many figures of gods, sages, people and animals, including…

dandin.s: Dandin was a Sanskrit writer of South India, probably active around 700, who is associated with the Pallava court at Kanchipuram. He wrote the Kavyadarsha, 'Mirror of Poetry', one of the most influential works of Sanskrit poetics, later adapted in Tamil, Kannada, Sinhala and…

diploma-ottonianum.s: The Diploma Ottonianum was a charter issued on 13 February 962 by the newly crowned emperor Otto I to Pope John XII. It confirmed the papacy's possession of the lands granted by the Carolingians, but also required that a newly elected pope swear an oath of loyalty before…

donation-of-constantine.s: The Donation of Constantine is a forged Roman imperial decree, probably composed in the eighth century, in which the emperor Constantine the Great appears to grant Pope Sylvester I and his successors authority over Rome and the western half of the empire. Used to support papal…

donation-of-pepin.s: The Donation of Pepin was the grant by the Frankish king Pepin the Short to the papacy of lands in central Italy taken from the Lombards, promised in 754 and carried out in 756. It gave the popes the former Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna and other territories, forming the…

dinant.s: Dinant is a town on the Meuse in the province of Namur, Belgium. In the Middle Ages it belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège and was famous for its brass and copperware, known as dinanderie.

despotate-of-the-morea.s: The Despotate of the Morea was a Byzantine province in the Peloponnese, ruled from Mistras by members of the imperial family with the title of despot. Growing from the fortresses ceded by the Franks in 1262, it reconquered most of the peninsula from the Principality of Achaea…

dalmau-de-queralt-count-of-santa-coloma.n: Dalmau de Queralt, Count of Santa Coloma
dalmau-de-queralt-count-of-santa-coloma.s: Dalmau de Queralt, Count of Santa Coloma, was a Catalan noble who served as viceroy of Catalonia for Philip IV. Enforcing the billeting of royal troops, he became hated, and he was killed in Barcelona during the Corpus de Sang riot of 7 June 1640, which began the Reapers' War.

dimitrie-cantemir.s: Dimitrie Cantemir was prince of Moldavia in 1693 and from 1710 to 1711, and a leading scholar. His alliance with Peter the Great ended in defeat on the Pruth in 1711, and he lived in Russia thereafter.

descriptio-moldaviae.s: Descriptio Moldaviae is a Latin description of Moldavia written by Dimitrie Cantemir in Russia around 1714–1716 at the request of the Berlin Academy. It covers the country's geography, government, customs and language, with an early map, and is a major source for its history.

dendera-temple-complex.s: The Dendera Temple complex lies on the west bank of the Nile near Qena in Upper Egypt. Its main temple, dedicated to the goddess Hathor, was begun in the last decades of the Ptolemaic period, under Ptolemy XII, and completed under Roman emperors.

dorgon.s: Dorgon was a Manchu prince, a son of Nurhaci, who served as regent for the young Shunzhi Emperor from 1643 to 1650. In 1644 he allied with the Ming general Wu Sangui, defeated the rebel Li Zicheng at Shanhai Pass and occupied Beijing, making it the Qing capital.

dashavatara-cave.s: The Dashavatara Cave, Cave 15 at Ellora in Maharashtra, is a two-storeyed rock-cut Hindu temple of the eighth century, named after its sculptures of the ten avatars of Vishnu. It also has large Shaiva reliefs.

dhanapala-poet.s: Dhanapala was a Jain poet and scholar at the Paramara court of Malwa under Vakpati Munja and Bhoja. He wrote the Sanskrit prose romance Tilakamanjari and the Paiyalacchi, a Prakrit lexicon completed in 972, which records that the Paramara army had just sacked Manyakheta, the…

digambara.s: Digambara, meaning 'sky-clad', is one of the two main traditions of Jainism, alongside the Svetambara. Its monks renounce all clothing, and it holds that women must be reborn as men to attain liberation and that the original scriptures were lost.

damrong-rajanubhab.s: Prince Damrong Rajanubhab was a son of King Mongkut and the leading administrator of Chulalongkorn's reforms in Siam. As Minister of the Interior from 1892 to 1915 he built the thesaphiban system, grouping provinces into monthon run by salaried officials in place of hereditary…

dhammayuttika-nikaya.s: The Dhammayuttika Nikaya, or Thammayut order, is a reformist order of Theravada Buddhist monks founded in Siam in 1833 by Prince Mongkut while he was a monk. Influenced by the Mon monastic tradition, it insisted on strict observance of the monastic code and on study of the…

daniel-salamanca.s: Daniel Salamanca was president of Bolivia from 1931 to 1934. Amid the economic crisis of the Great Depression, he pursued a hard line over the disputed Chaco region and in 1932 led Bolivia into the Chaco War with Paraguay.

david-toro.s: David Toro was a Bolivian army officer who served in the Chaco War and became president after a military coup in May 1936. His government proclaimed 'military socialism', created a ministry of labour, founded the state oil company YPFB and in 1937 confiscated the holdings of…

day-of-the-sea.s: The Day of the Sea is a Bolivian national commemoration held every 23 March, the anniversary of the death of Eduardo Abaroa at the Battle of Topáter in 1879, at the start of the War of the Pacific. It mourns the loss of Bolivia's Pacific coast to Chile and affirms its claim to…

democratic-progressive-party.s: The Democratic Progressive Party is a Taiwanese political party founded on 28 September 1986, while martial law was still in force, by opponents of Kuomintang one-party rule. It campaigned for democracy and a distinct Taiwanese identity.

daniel-noboa.s: Daniel Noboa is an Ecuadorian businessman and politician, the son of the banana magnate Álvaro Noboa. He won the early election of 2023 that followed Guillermo Lasso's dissolution of the National Assembly, becoming one of the youngest presidents in Ecuador's history.

divine-comedy.s: The Divine Comedy is a long narrative poem by Dante Alighieri, written in the Florentine vernacular from about 1308 until his death in 1321. In three parts, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, it describes the poet's journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, guided by Virgil…

discourses-on-livy.s: The Discourses on Livy are a work of political theory by Niccolò Machiavelli, written around 1517 and published in 1531. Taking the first ten books of Livy's history of Rome as a starting point, Machiavelli analysed how republics are founded, expanded and preserved, praising…

donatello.s: Donatello (c. 1386–1466) was a Florentine sculptor of the early Renaissance.

dominican-republic.s: The Dominican Republic is a country occupying the eastern two-thirds of the island of Hispaniola, with its capital at Santo Domingo. Spain's first colony in the Americas, it was ruled by Haiti from 1822 and declared independence on 27 February 1844.

donald-trump.s: Donald Trump (born 1946) is an American businessman and Republican politician who served as the 45th president of the United States from 2017 to 2021 and became the 47th president in January 2025. His administrations restricted immigration and raised tariffs; in his second…

dalia-grybauskaite.s: Dalia Grybauskaitė is a Lithuanian politician who was president of Lithuania from 2009 to 2019, the first woman in the office and the first to be re-elected for a second consecutive term. An economist, she previously served as finance minister and as European Commissioner for…

democratic-revolutionary-party.s: The Democratic Revolutionary Party is a Panamanian political party founded in 1979 by Omar Torrijos as the political arm of his military regime. It supported Manuel Noriega in the 1980s but, after the American invasion, transformed itself into a democratic centre-left party.

dina-boluarte.s: Dina Boluarte is a Peruvian lawyer and politician who became Peru's first woman president in December 2022, when as vice-president she succeeded Pedro Castillo after his removal. Protests against her government in the following months were suppressed with dozens of deaths, and…

dubrovnik.s: Dubrovnik is a city on the southern Dalmatian coast of Croatia, known historically as Ragusa. From the Middle Ages until 1808 it was the centre of the independent maritime Republic of Ragusa, a rival of Venice that traded across the Mediterranean and the Balkans.

dundo-maroje.s: Dundo Maroje is a prose comedy by the Ragusan writer Marin Držić, first performed in Dubrovnik in 1551. It follows an old merchant, Maroje, who travels to Rome to recover money squandered by his son, and satirises greed and social pretension.

dubrovacko-primorje.s: Dubrovačko primorje, the Dubrovnik Littoral, is the coastal strip north-west of Dubrovnik between the city and the Pelješac peninsula, in present-day Croatia. The Republic of Ragusa acquired it from the Bosnian king Stephen Ostoja in 1399, linking its territory around the city…

dahabshiil.s: Dahabshiil is a money-transfer and banking company founded in 1970 by Mohamed Said Duale in Burao, in what is now Somaliland. It grew into the largest remittance company in the Horn of Africa, moving money from the Somali diaspora to families at home and operating in many…

dahir-riyale-kahin.s: Dahir Riyale Kahin is a Somaliland politician who was president of Somaliland from 2002 to 2010. Vice-president under Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal, he succeeded him on his death in May 2002 and won the 2003 election by about 80 votes, a result the opposition accepted.

dhulbahante.s: The Dhulbahante are a Somali clan of the Harti branch of the Darod, living mainly in the Sool region and parts of Sanaag and Togdheer. Their territory lies within the borders of former British Somaliland, but many Dhulbahante have rejected the authority of Somaliland, and…
